79.problem: You have a sorted array and a number to find. Return the number’s index. If it is missing, return -1.
79.assumptions: The array is already sorted. If the number appears more than once, this version may return any matching index.

example.explanation: Start with indices 0 through 4. The midpoint is 2, whose value is 8, so retain indices 3 through 4. The next midpoint is 3 and its value is 12.

79.baseline: Start at the first element and check each value. This works, but a missing target makes you read the whole array.
79.approach:
Suppose the middle value is 8 and you need 12. Because the array is sorted, every value before 8 is also too small. You can skip that whole part.

If the middle value is too large, do the same thing on the other side. Keep checking the middle of the part that remains. Each check either finds the answer or removes about half the remaining elements.
steps: Use low and high to mark the first and last positions you still need to check.
Calculate mid. If arr[mid] is the target, return mid.
If the middle value is too small, set low to mid + 1. Otherwise, set high to mid - 1.
Stop when low passes high. There is nowhere left to look, so return -1.
79.time: O(log n): the part you search becomes about half as large after each miss.
79.space: O(1): only low, high and mid are needed.
pitfalls: Use mid + 1 and mid - 1 after a miss. Keeping mid can make the same check repeat forever.
Use low <= high so the final remaining element is checked.
This method needs sorted input. Sorting just to search once would add extra work and change the original indices.

rows: 8 is smaller than 12. Move low to 3.

reference.title: binary search
reference.approach: linear search first, then iterative binary search

12.problem: Choose Java collections according to the operation you need: ordered traversal, uniqueness, key lookup, a stack or queue, or repeated extraction of the smallest item.
12.assumptions: This lesson demonstrates a frequency table. HashMap iteration order is unspecified; sort keys explicitly when output order matters.

example.explanation: The first 4 creates a count of one. Each later 4 increments that entry. The final table has three keys even though the input has six values.

12.baseline: You can count each distinct value by scanning the whole array again, using O(n²) time in the worst case. A map remembers previous work.
12.approach: Use ArrayList for indexed sequences, HashSet for membership, HashMap for key/value associations, ArrayDeque for stacks and queues, and PriorityQueue for smallest-first extraction. A TreeMap provides sorted keys at O(log d) per operation. For frequency counting, increment one map entry per element.
steps: Create an empty map.
For every value, combine one with the existing count.
Read counts with getOrDefault(value, 0). Copy keys into a TreeMap when sorted display is required.
12.time: Expected O(n) for the frequency table using ordinary HashMap operations.
12.space: O(d), where d is the number of distinct values.
pitfalls: Use equals for object equality; == compares object references.
PriorityQueue iteration is not sorted; repeatedly poll to get priority order.
ArrayDeque rejects null. Use push/pop consistently for a stack and offer/poll for a queue.
List<Integer>.remove(1) removes index 1; remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes a value.

13.problem: Count the decimal digits of an integer, ignoring its sign.
13.assumptions: Zero has one digit. Inputs fit in a Java int.

example.explanation: The absolute value becomes 12040. Repeated divisions by ten leave 1204, 120, 12, 1, then 0, so five digits were removed.

13.baseline: Converting the magnitude to a string and taking its length works, but creates an extra character representation.
13.approach: Each integer division by ten removes the least significant decimal digit. A do-while loop counts zero correctly without a special return.
steps: Promote to long before taking the absolute value.
Increment the count once for each division by ten.
Stop when the remaining magnitude becomes zero.
13.time: O(d), where d is the number of decimal digits.
pitfalls: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) overflows as an int; promotion must happen first.
A while loop without a special case returns zero digits for zero.

14.problem: Reverse the decimal digits of a signed 32-bit integer. Return zero if the reversed value cannot fit in an int.
14.assumptions: Leading zeroes of the reversed number are discarded. The sign is preserved.

example.explanation: The remainders are 0, -2, and -1 in Java. Building result = result * 10 + remainder gives 0, -2, then -21.

14.baseline: Reverse a string representation and parse it, taking special care with the sign and overflow.
14.approach: Remove digits with division and append them to a long accumulator. There are at most ten digits, so the accumulator fits in long; check the int bounds before returning.
steps: Take n % 10 as the next digit.
Append it to the accumulator and divide n by ten.
Check the final value against the signed int range.
pitfalls: Do not multiply an int accumulator before checking overflow.
Reversing 120 gives 21, not 021 as a numeric value.

15.problem: Decide whether an integer reads the same from left to right and right to left in decimal.
15.assumptions: Negative integers are not palindromes; zero is a palindrome.

example.explanation: Reversing its digits produces 1221 again, equal to the original number.

15.baseline: Convert to a string and compare characters from both ends, using O(d) space for the string.
15.approach: Reject negatives, then construct the reversed number in long and compare it with the original. A long safely holds the reverse of any nonnegative int.
steps: Save the original value.
Reverse its digits into a long accumulator.
Return whether both numbers are equal.
pitfalls: A minus sign is not ignored in this variant.
A positive number ending in zero cannot be a palindrome unless it is zero itself.

16.problem: Find the greatest common divisor of two integers.
16.assumptions: The result is nonnegative. This implementation defines gcd(0, 0) as 0 and returns long to cover Integer.MIN_VALUE.

example.explanation: Euclid transforms (48,18) into (18,12), then (12,6), then (6,0). The final nonzero value is 6.

16.baseline: Try every positive divisor up to the smaller magnitude. This can take linear time in that magnitude.
16.approach: The common divisors of a and b are exactly the common divisors of b and a % b. Repeating that reduction preserves the answer while rapidly shrinking the inputs.
steps: Normalize magnitudes after promoting to long.
Replace (a,b) with (b,a%b) until b is zero.
Return a.
16.time: O(log(min(|a|, |b|))) when both are nonzero; constant work when one is zero.
pitfalls: Avoid division by zero by checking y before taking the remainder.
If you later compute lcm, divide by gcd before multiplying and handle zero explicitly.

17.problem: Check whether a nonnegative integer equals the sum of each decimal digit raised to the number of digits.
17.assumptions: This is the general Armstrong-number definition, not only the three-digit version.

example.explanation: There are three digits: 1³ + 5³ + 3³ = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153.

17.baseline: Extract the digits as a string and raise each digit to the string length. That works but needs extra storage.
17.approach: Count the digits, then scan them again. Compute each small integer power with multiplication to avoid floating-point rounding.
steps: Count digits with zero treated as one digit.
For each digit, multiply it by itself d times.
Sum using long and compare with the original.
17.time: O(d²) with the small repeated-multiplication power calculation.
pitfalls: Do not assume every input has three digits.
Using Math.pow introduces floating-point values into an exact integer comparison.

18.problem: Return all positive divisors of a positive integer in ascending order.
18.assumptions: n must be positive; zero has infinitely many nonzero integer divisors and is rejected.

example.explanation: Pairs (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), and (6,6) cover every divisor. Include the square-root divisor only once.

18.baseline: Check every value from 1 through n, requiring O(n) divisibility tests.
18.approach: Every divisor below the square root has a partner above it. Collect the smaller partners in increasing order and the larger partners in decreasing order, then reverse the larger list.
steps: Loop while i <= n / i to avoid squaring overflow.
When divisible, add i and add n/i only if it differs.
Append the larger partners in reverse order.
18.time: O(√n + d), where d is the number of returned divisors.
pitfalls: A perfect square must not emit its square root twice.
Testing i*i <= n with int arithmetic can overflow for large inputs.

19.problem: Decide whether an integer is prime: it must be greater than one and have no positive divisor other than one and itself.

example.explanation: After excluding divisibility by 2, test 3 and 5. Neither divides 29, and any factor larger than √29 would need a smaller partner already tested.

19.baseline: Count divisors from 1 through n, which takes O(n) time.
19.approach: A composite number has a divisor no larger than its square root. Handle 2 separately, reject other even values, and test only odd candidates.
steps: Reject n < 2; accept 2.
Reject even n.
Test odd divisors while d <= n/d.
19.time: O(√n) trial divisions in the worst case.
pitfalls: One is neither prime nor composite.
A square such as 49 requires testing its square root, so use <= rather than <.

24.assumptions: n is a nonnegative int. Return long so the sum fits for every valid input.

example.explanation: Pair 1 with 5 and 2 with 4; each pair totals 6, with 3 left over. The formula gives 5 × 6 / 2 = 15.

24.baseline: A loop or recursion that adds one number per step costs O(n) time; recursive addition also uses O(n) stack frames.
24.approach: Pair the first and last terms. There are n terms and each has average (n+1)/2, giving n(n+1)/2. Promote before addition and multiplication.
steps: Reject negative n.
Compute n * (n + 1) in long.
Divide the even product by two.
pitfalls: n*(n+1) overflows int well before the result is large by long standards.
The empty sum for n=0 is zero.

25.problem: Compute n factorial, the product of the integers from 1 through n.
25.assumptions: This long-returning implementation supports 0 through 20. Larger factorials need BigInteger.

example.explanation: The recursive chain is 5 × factorial(4), continuing until factorial(0)=1, then multiplying while calls return.

25.baseline: Multiply iteratively from 2 to n. This has the same arithmetic work and avoids recursion-stack space.
25.approach: The recurrence factorial(n)=n×factorial(n−1) mirrors the product definition. The base case must be one because one is multiplication’s identity.
steps: Validate the range so overflow cannot silently produce an answer.
Use 0! = 1 as the base case.
Multiply n by the factorial of n−1.
25.time: O(n) for this bounded fixed-width implementation.
25.space: O(n) recursion stack; an iterative version uses O(1).
pitfalls: Returning zero at the base case makes every factorial zero.
21! exceeds long; use arbitrary precision rather than allowing wraparound.

26.assumptions: The array may be empty. Element values and duplicates are unrestricted.

example.explanation: Swap positions 0 and 3, giving [4,2,3,1]. Swap positions 1 and 2, giving [4,3,2,1].

26.baseline: Copy elements into a new array in reverse order, using O(n) additional storage.
26.approach: The left and right endpoints belong in each other’s positions. After swapping, the only unfinished work is the smaller interior interval. This version uses recursion to expose that shrinking subproblem.
steps: Call the helper with both end indices.
Stop when the indices meet or cross.
Swap the endpoints, then recurse inward.
26.space: O(n) recursion stack. Replacing recursion with a while loop reduces extra space to O(1).
pitfalls: The middle element in an odd-length array stays in place.
Do not recurse without advancing both endpoints.
Prefer iteration for large arrays to avoid StackOverflowError.
tests: int[] a={1,2,3,4}; reverse(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{4,3,2,1});

27.problem: Check whether a string is a palindrome by comparing characters from its ends.
27.assumptions: This version is case-sensitive and compares UTF-16 code units exactly, including spaces and punctuation.

example.explanation: Compare r with r, a with a, and c with c. The remaining middle e cannot break the palindrome.

27.baseline: Reverse the string into a new buffer and compare it with the original, using O(n) extra space.
27.approach: A string is a palindrome when its endpoints match and its interior is also a palindrome. A mismatch lets us return immediately.
steps: Start at the first and last positions.
Return true when the interval has zero or one character.
Otherwise compare endpoints and recurse inward only if they match.
27.time: O(n) comparisons in the worst case.
27.space: O(n) recursion stack; iteration uses O(1).
pitfalls: Clarify whether a platform wants punctuation removed or case ignored; that is a different normalization step.
Supplementary Unicode characters require code-point handling rather than char indexing.

28.problem: Return the nth Fibonacci number with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.
28.assumptions: The implementation supports 0 through 92, the largest index whose Fibonacci value fits in signed long.

example.explanation: Starting with 0 and 1, successive sums are 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 13.

28.baseline: The direct recursive formula computes the same smaller values repeatedly, taking exponential time. Memoization reduces that to O(n) time and space.
28.approach: Only the previous two values are needed. Advance the pair instead of storing the entire sequence. The loop computes up to F(n), avoiding an unnecessary F(93) overflow when n=92.
steps: Handle n=0 directly.
Initialize the pair to F(0) and F(1).
For each index from 2 through n, compute the sum and shift the pair.
pitfalls: State the indexing convention; some sources call the first 1 term one.
Int overflows at F(47); long overflows at F(93).

1.problem: Read a value from standard input and write it to standard output. The important distinction is between input data and explanatory output intended only for a person.
1.assumptions: This introductory example reads one signed integer token and echoes it. Adapt parsing to the exact format specified by a practice judge.

example.explanation: Scanner reads the token 42 as an int; converting that value back to decimal gives the same text.

1.baseline: Hardcoding the example produces the right output for only one input. A solution must parse the supplied data.
1.approach: Scanner is convenient for learning token-based input. For large inputs, BufferedReader plus tokenization avoids much of Scanner’s parsing overhead. Print only what the problem requests.
steps: Create a reader for the input.
Read a value using the correct type.
Write the result without extra prompts on an online judge.
1.time: O(L), where L is the input length examined by the parser.
1.space: O(L) for this String-based test helper; a stream-based program need not retain all input.
pitfalls: nextInt leaves a following newline; a later nextLine can therefore return an empty string.
Use long for values outside the int range.
Do not print “Enter a number” when a judge expects only the answer.

2.problem: Understand arrays as indexed collections and strings as text sequences. Practise reading every element without going outside the valid index range.
2.assumptions: The example sums an int array; strings in Java are immutable UTF-16 sequences.

example.explanation: Read indices 0, 1, and 2. Accumulating 3 + 5 − 2 gives 6.

2.baseline: Separate variables work only for a fixed number of values. An array gives one uniform way to process an arbitrary-sized sequence.
2.approach: Array indices run from zero through length−1. A traversal can use an enhanced for loop when the index itself is unnecessary. Strings use length() and charAt(index), while arrays use the length field.
steps: Initialize an accumulator.
Read each array element once.
Use a long accumulator when the sum may exceed int.
2.time: O(n) for a complete array traversal; indexed access is O(1).
pitfalls: The last index is length−1, not length.
Assigning one array variable to another shares the array; use clone when you need a copy.
Use StringBuilder for repeated text concatenation in a loop.

3.problem: Choose numeric types that can represent both the input and intermediate results.
3.assumptions: The example multiplies two ints and returns their exact product as long.

example.explanation: The result exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE. Promoting one operand before multiplication makes Java compute the product as a long.

3.baseline: Storing a*b into a long after int multiplication is too late: overflow has already happened.
3.approach: The arithmetic type is decided from the operands, not the destination variable. Cast before the operation. Floating-point types represent approximations and should not replace exact integer arithmetic without a reason.
steps: Check the input range.
Estimate the largest intermediate result.
Promote an operand before the risky operation.
pitfalls: Java int and long arithmetic normally wraps on overflow; it does not automatically throw.
Integer division truncates toward zero. Use a floating-point operand when a fractional answer is intended.
For values beyond long, use BigInteger.

4.problem: Select exactly one branch according to whether an integer is negative, zero, or positive.
4.assumptions: This lesson demonstrates mutually exclusive conditions.

example.explanation: The first condition n<0 is true, so the later branches are skipped.

4.baseline: Three independent if statements can work for disjoint tests, but they do not express that exactly one branch should run.
4.approach: An if/else-if/else chain evaluates conditions in order and stops after the first match. Put narrow conditions before broader conditions that would otherwise swallow them.
steps: Test the first case.
Use else-if for the next mutually exclusive case.
Use else for the remaining inputs.
4.time: O(1) for a fixed number of conditions.
pitfalls: Use == for comparison and = for assignment.
Boundary values belong in exactly one branch; test zero and threshold values.

5.problem: Choose an operation from a small fixed set using switch.
5.assumptions: The example supports integer addition and subtraction; arithmetic is promoted to long. Unknown operators are rejected.

example.explanation: The + case returns the sum immediately. No other case runs.

5.baseline: An if/else chain is equivalent and useful for conditions that are not equality checks against fixed values.
5.approach: Switch makes a finite set of discrete choices explicit. In a traditional switch, break or return prevents accidental fall-through. A default branch handles unsupported inputs.
steps: Switch on the operator.
Return the result for each supported case.
Reject unsupported operators in default.
5.time: O(1) for this fixed set of operators.
pitfalls: Traditional cases can fall through without break or return.
If division is added, specify integer versus floating-point behavior and handle a zero divisor.
tests: boolean failed=false; try { calculate('*',2,3); } catch(IllegalArgumentException e) { failed=true; } assert failed;

6.problem: Repeat a computation a known number of times with a for loop.
6.assumptions: The example returns the first n positive integers; n must be nonnegative.

example.explanation: The loop starts at 1, includes 4, and stops when the counter becomes 5.

6.baseline: Writing one statement per item cannot adapt to a changing n.
6.approach: A for loop groups initialization, continuation condition, and update in one place. The loop invariant here is that the list contains exactly 1 through i−1 before iteration i.
steps: Start the counter at one.
Continue while i <= n.
Append i and increment the counter.
6.space: O(n) for the returned list; O(1) auxiliary state.
pitfalls: Distinguish < n from <= n.
Very large n can exceed memory and, at Integer.MAX_VALUE, an int loop counter can wrap; this educational list example assumes a feasible list size.

7.problem: Repeat while a condition remains true, updating the state so the loop eventually stops.
7.assumptions: The example sums decimal digits of a nonnegative int.

example.explanation: Extract 3, then 2, then 0, then 4. Their sum is 9.

7.baseline: Convert to text and iterate over characters, using an extra string representation.
7.approach: A while loop is useful when the number of iterations follows from changing state. Dividing by ten makes the remaining value smaller on every iteration.
steps: Initialize the sum to zero.
While digits remain, add n % 10.
Remove that digit with n /= 10.
7.time: O(d), where d is the number of digits.
pitfalls: Forgetting the state update can create an infinite loop.
A while loop may execute zero times; a do-while loop executes at least once.

8.problem: Understand Java’s pass-by-value semantics for primitives and object references.
8.assumptions: Every parameter receives a copy of a value. For arrays, the copied value is a reference to the same array object.

example.explanation: The first assignment changes the shared array element. Reassigning the local parameter to a new array does not replace the caller’s reference, so the caller still sees [9].

8.baseline: Trying to swap caller variables by reassigning two parameters does not work in Java, because only local copies change.
8.approach: Distinguish changing an object from changing the variable that refers to it. Mutations through a copied reference affect the shared object; rebinding the parameter affects only the method.
steps: Receive a copy of the caller’s reference.
Mutate the referenced object to demonstrate shared state.
Rebind the local reference and observe that the caller is unchanged by the rebind.
pitfalls: Java does not switch to pass-by-reference for objects.
Return a new object explicitly when the caller should replace its reference.

9.problem: Analyze how the number of operations grows with input size rather than relying on a particular machine’s timing.
9.assumptions: The example counts all index pairs i<j in an array of length n.

example.explanation: The outer iterations contribute 3, 2, 1, and 0 pairs. Their total is 6 = n(n−1)/2.

9.baseline: Measuring a few elapsed times can suggest a trend but does not establish a growth bound.
9.approach: Count the inner-loop executions: (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1. This is a quadratic polynomial, so its dominant growth is Θ(n²), despite the changing inner-loop bound. A formula computes the same count in O(1), but does not enumerate the pairs.
steps: Write the number of iterations for each outer-loop position.
Add those counts as a sum.
Keep the dominant term and distinguish time from storage.
pitfalls: Not all nested loops imply quadratic time: a shared monotonic pointer can advance only O(n) times overall.
Include recursion-stack memory when analyzing space.
Big-O is a bound, not an exact operation count.

10.problem: Build a text pattern by identifying what each row contains.
10.assumptions: Codolio groups pattern practice into one entry. This example covers a centered pyramid of height n; the same row/column reasoning extends to other shapes.

example.explanation: Row r, starting at zero, has n−r−1 leading spaces and 2r+1 stars. For n=3 those counts are (2,1), (1,3), and (0,5).

10.baseline: Hardcoding each row works for one height only and hides the rule that generates the shape.
10.approach: Derive spaces and symbols separately before writing loops. Express both counts as functions of the row number, then build each row with those exact counts.
steps: For row r, append n−r−1 spaces.
Append 2r+1 stars.
Separate rows with newlines, avoiding an extra newline after the last row.
10.time: Θ(n²), proportional to the number of output characters.
pitfalls: Inspect spaces as well as visible symbols; formatting is part of the answer.
One pattern entry can contain many exercises; derive each shape rather than treating this pyramid as every possible pattern.
String.repeat requires Java 11 or newer.

11.problem: Translate common C++ STL roles into Java collections and utility methods.
11.assumptions: This is a language-bridge lesson. The example sorts an array; it does not attempt to reproduce C++ iterator syntax in Java.

example.explanation: Sorting places the duplicate ones first, then 3 and 4. The input is copied so the caller’s original order remains intact.

11.baseline: Implementing every container and sorting routine from scratch is useful for learning, but unnecessary for most problem-solving tasks.
11.approach: Use ArrayList for a dynamic sequence, HashMap or TreeMap for dictionaries, HashSet or TreeSet for sets, ArrayDeque for stack/queue operations, and PriorityQueue for a heap. Arrays.sort handles arrays; List.sort handles lists.
steps: Choose the collection by its required operations and ordering.
Copy the input if mutation is not allowed.
Call the standard sorting utility and return the copy.
11.time: Sorting is typically O(n log n); precise algorithm guarantees depend on the Java version and array element type. Copying costs O(n).
11.space: O(n) for the returned copy, plus the sorting implementation’s workspace.
pitfalls: Java PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default, unlike the common C++ priority_queue default.
Use Integer.compare(a,b), not a-b, in comparators that might overflow.
Do not apply object comparators directly to primitive int[] arrays.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; assert Arrays.equals(sortedCopy(a),new int[]{1,1,3,4}); assert a[0]==4;

20.problem: Use recursion to produce a fixed message.
20.assumptions: n is nonnegative. The implementation collects output in a list so it can be tested; printing each added item gives the corresponding console exercise.

example.explanation: Each call reduces n by one. Appending before the recursive call emits one copy per level.

20.baseline: A loop produces the same sequence without recursion-stack overhead.
20.approach: A recursive solution needs a base case, one unit of work, and a smaller subproblem. The position of the work relative to the recursive call determines output order.
steps: Return immediately when n is zero.
Perform the append before or after recursion according to the desired order.
Recurse with n−1 so the base case is reachable.
20.space: O(n) for the recursion stack and O(n) for the result.
pitfalls: Large n can overflow the call stack; prefer iteration when recursion is not the lesson.
Do not confuse the return order with the order in which recursive calls begin.

29.problem: Understand hash-based lookup and build a frequency table.
29.assumptions: HashMap provides expected constant-time basic operations under normal hashing assumptions; it does not preserve sorted order.

example.explanation: The map accumulates three occurrences of 5, two of 2, and one of 9. Repeated values update an existing key.

29.baseline: For each value, scan the entire input to count matches. Repeating that work can take O(n²) time.
29.approach: Hashing maps a key to a bucket so a lookup can avoid scanning all previous keys. Collisions still require resolution; equal hash codes do not mean equal keys. A frequency table stores one count per distinct value.
steps: Create an empty map.
For each element, insert one or increment its existing count.
Query a missing key with getOrDefault(key,0).
29.time: Expected O(n) to build the table.
pitfalls: A direct-indexed array is useful only when the key range is small and known.
Do not assume HashMap iteration gives numeric order.
Mutable keys can become unfindable if their equality/hashCode-relevant state changes after insertion.

30.problem: Count how often every distinct integer appears in an array.
30.assumptions: HashMap provides expected constant-time basic operations under normal hashing assumptions; it does not preserve sorted order.

example.explanation: The map accumulates three occurrences of 5, two of 2, and one of 9. Repeated values update an existing key.

30.baseline: For each value, scan the entire input to count matches. Repeating that work can take O(n²) time.
30.approach: Hashing maps a key to a bucket so a lookup can avoid scanning all previous keys. Collisions still require resolution; equal hash codes do not mean equal keys. A frequency table stores one count per distinct value.
steps: Create an empty map.
For each element, insert one or increment its existing count.
Query a missing key with getOrDefault(key,0).
30.time: Expected O(n) to build the table.
pitfalls: A direct-indexed array is useful only when the key range is small and known.
Do not assume HashMap iteration gives numeric order.
Mutable keys can become unfindable if their equality/hashCode-relevant state changes after insertion.

31.problem: Find the values with the highest and lowest occurrence counts in an array.
31.assumptions: For ties choose the smaller value. The input must be nonempty. Return [mostFrequent, leastFrequent].

example.explanation: Counts are 5→3, 2→2, and 9→1. Thus 5 is most frequent and 9 is least frequent.

31.baseline: Count each candidate by a full scan, taking O(n²) time.
31.approach: Build a frequency table once, then compare its entries. Tie-breaking is part of the contract and must be explicit because HashMap order is unspecified.
steps: Count every distinct value.
Initialize both answers from an actual input value.
Replace an answer on a better frequency or an equal frequency with a smaller key.
pitfalls: Clarify whether the question wants element values or frequency counts.
Initializing to zero fails when zero is absent or every input is negative.

32.problem: Selection sort repeatedly places the smallest remaining value at the next output position.
32.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

32.baseline: An all-pairs swapping scheme is harder to reason about; separate finding the minimum from performing one final swap.
32.approach: The prefix before i is already sorted and contains the globally smallest i values. Choose the minimum from the remaining suffix to extend that invariant.
steps: For each destination i, scan i through n−1 for the smallest value.
Swap that value into i.
Advance i; the completed prefix never needs to move again.
32.time: Θ(n²) comparisons for every input order.
pitfalls: Ordinary swapping selection sort is not stable.
Find the minimum index, not merely its value, so duplicates can be swapped correctly.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

33.problem: Bubble sort moves the largest unfinished value to the right through adjacent swaps.
33.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

33.baseline: Repeatedly scan all n elements n times. This works but wastes comparisons after the suffix is already sorted.
33.approach: After a left-to-right pass over the unfinished prefix, its maximum is at the right boundary. Shrink that boundary, and stop early when a pass makes no swaps.
steps: Compare adjacent pairs in the unfinished prefix.
Swap only if the left value is larger.
Shrink the right boundary; stop if the whole pass was unchanged.
33.time: O(n²) worst case; O(n) when already sorted with this early exit.
pitfalls: Using >= instead of > swaps equal items and loses stability.
The adjacent pair accesses j+1, so j must stay below end.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

34.problem: Insertion sort extends a sorted prefix by inserting the next element into its correct position.
34.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

34.baseline: A separate sorted list can accept each element at the correct position, but requires extra storage.
34.approach: Save the next value, shift all larger prefix elements one place right, then put the saved value in the gap. The shift preserves the relative order of equal values.
steps: Start with the one-element prefix.
Save a[i] before shifting.
Move larger predecessors right and write the saved value into the final gap.
34.time: O(n²) worst case; O(n) for already sorted input.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite the insertion value while shifting.
Test j>=0 before indexing a[j].
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

35.problem: Merge sort divides an array into smaller halves and merges sorted halves back together.
35.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

35.baseline: Quadratic sorts are simple, but their comparison count grows too quickly on large inputs.
35.approach: Once both halves are sorted, repeatedly choosing the smaller front element produces the entire merged range in linear time. There are logarithmically many division levels.
steps: Recursively sort the half-open ranges [lo,mid) and [mid,hi).
Merge into a reusable temporary array.
Copy the merged range back; choose the left element on ties for stability.
35.space: O(n) temporary storage plus O(log n) stack.
pitfalls: Do not mix inclusive and half-open boundaries.
Allocate one reusable buffer instead of allocating a new buffer per merge.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

36.problem: Express bubble sort recursively by sorting one fewer position after each pass.
36.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

36.baseline: The iterative bubble-sort loop performs the same passes without recursive frames.
36.approach: One pass settles the largest unfinished value at the end. The recursive subproblem therefore excludes that final position. The array itself is shared; it does not need to be copied.
steps: Stop when the unfinished length is at most one.
Perform one adjacent-swap pass.
If something changed, recursively sort the prefix of length n−1.
36.time: O(n²) worst case, O(n) for an already sorted input.
36.space: O(n) recursion stack in the worst case.
pitfalls: Recursion does not make bubble sort asymptotically faster.
Use an iterative sort for large n to avoid exhausting the call stack.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

37.problem: Express insertion sort recursively by sorting a prefix before inserting its last element.
37.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

37.baseline: Iterative insertion sort avoids stack overhead while making the same comparisons and shifts.
37.approach: First solve the smaller problem: sort the first n−1 elements. Only the final element can then be out of place, so insert it into that sorted prefix.
steps: Stop at an unfinished length of zero or one.
Recursively sort the first n−1 elements.
Shift larger predecessors right and place the saved last value in the gap.
37.time: O(n²) worst case; O(n) comparisons on sorted input.
pitfalls: Do the recursive call before insertion; otherwise the prefix is not guaranteed sorted.
Equal elements should not be shifted past each other if stability matters.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

38.problem: Quicksort partitions values around a pivot and recursively sorts the remaining ranges.
38.assumptions: Sort ascending in place; empty arrays, negative values, and duplicates are supported.

example.explanation: The sorted output contains the same multiset of values; the two equal ones remain represented separately.

38.baseline: Repeatedly finding the next minimum takes O(n²) comparisons. Quicksort aims to partition many values at once.
38.approach: This three-way partition maintains values less than the pivot, equal to it, and greater than it. All equal values are finished together, which avoids repeated work on duplicate-heavy inputs. Choosing the middle value is simple but does not guarantee balanced partitions.
steps: Save the pivot value before swaps can move it.
Partition with lt, i, and gt; after a swap from the right, inspect the new a[i] again.
Recursively sort the less-than and greater-than ranges.
38.time: O(n log n) with balanced partitions; O(n²) worst case. Random pivot selection can provide expected O(n log n).
38.space: O(log n) stack when balanced, O(n) in the worst case.
pitfalls: This implementation is not stable.
Do not advance i after swapping a greater value with gt; the incoming value remains unclassified.
A middle-position pivot is not necessarily the median value.
tests: int[] a={4,1,3,1}; sort(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,1,3,4});

Random rng=new Random(7); for(int t=0;t<100;t++){int[] x=new int[rng.nextInt(40)]; for(int i=0;i<x.length;i++)x[i]=rng.nextInt(21)-10; int[] expected=x.clone(); Arrays.sort(expected); sort(x); assert Arrays.equals(x,expected);}

39.problem: Return the largest value in an array.
39.assumptions: The input must be nonempty. Negative values are supported.

example.explanation: Start with -4. Seeing -1 raises the maximum; -7 leaves it unchanged.

39.baseline: Sorting places the largest value at the end but takes more work and may alter the input.
39.approach: After processing each prefix, keep its maximum. Comparing one new value is sufficient to extend that invariant.
steps: Initialize from the first element.
Scan the remaining elements.
Replace the maximum only when the new value is larger.
39.time: Θ(n), since every element may contain the maximum.
pitfalls: Initializing to zero fails on an all-negative input.
An empty array has no largest element; define a clear contract.

40.problem: Find the second-largest distinct number in the array. Return -1 if it does not exist.
40.assumptions: Repeated copies of the largest number do not count as second place. Negative numbers are allowed.

example.explanation: Before 9 arrives, 7 is the largest and 5 is second. When 9 becomes the largest, the old largest, 7, takes second place.

40.baseline: Sort a copy. Walk backwards past any repeated largest values; the next value is the answer.
40.baselineTime: O(n log n), with O(n) space for the copy.

better.explanation: First find the largest number. Scan again and find the largest number strictly below it. Two scans still take linear time.

40.approach:
Keep two places: largest and second largest. A new largest pushes the old largest into second place. A smaller number can improve second place without changing first.

Use a separate flag for whether second place is filled. Starting second at zero must not make zero a candidate in an all-negative array.
steps: Start largest at the first value; second place is empty.
Read each remaining value and update the two places. Ignore equal largest values.
Return second when filled, otherwise -1.
pitfalls: Do not count duplicate maximums twice.
The return value -1 can also be a valid second-largest value; that ambiguity is part of this problem’s return convention.

reference.title: second-largest element
reference.approach: sorting, two scans, then one scan

tests: assert secondLargest(new int[]{7,7})==-1;assert secondLargest(new int[]{})==-1;assert secondLargest(new int[]{5})==-1;

Random random=new Random(40);for(int t=0;t<300;t++){int[] a=new int[random.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=random.nextInt(21)-10;int expected=secondLargestSorted(a);assert secondLargest(a)==expected;assert secondLargestTwoPass(a)==expected;}

41.problem: Check whether the numbers are in ascending order. Equal neighbours are allowed.
41.assumptions: Equal adjacent values are allowed. Empty and single-element arrays are sorted.

example.explanation: 1 does not exceed 2, the two 2s are equal, and 2 does not exceed 4. No pair goes downhill.

41.baseline: Compare each number with every number after it. If an earlier number is larger, return false.
41.approach:
Imagine walking along the array. You may move up or stay level, but you must never move down. If every step follows that rule, no later value can be smaller than an earlier one.

So compare only neighbours. The first downward step is enough to return false.
steps: Start at index one.
Reject when a[i−1] > a[i].
Accept after reaching the end.
pitfalls: Using >= would incorrectly reject duplicates.
This checks sortedness, not whether the array is a rotation of a sorted array.
tests: Random random=new Random(41);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[random.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=random.nextInt(5);assert sorted(a)==sortedPairs(a);}

reference.title: sorted-array check
reference.approach: all-pairs checking, then adjacent comparisons

42.problem: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the number of distinct values.
42.assumptions: Only the first returned-length positions are meaningful; the array object keeps its original size.

example.explanation: Keep the first 1, skip the next 1, write 2 into position 1, skip its duplicate, then write 3 into position 2.

42.baseline: Collect distinct values in a temporary list. Before adding a value, search that list to check whether it is already there. Copy the list back.
42.approach:
Use the front of the same array as your answer. write points to its next free place; read looks for the next new value.

Compare with the last value you kept. If it differs, copy it to write and move write forward. You only copy leftwards or stay in place, so you never lose an unread value.
steps: Return zero for empty input.
Keep the first value.
Write a new value only when it differs from the most recently retained value.
pitfalls: The input must already be sorted.
Do not inspect the unused suffix as if it were part of the result.
tests: int[] a={1,1,2,2,3}; int n=unique(a); assert n==3; assert Arrays.equals(Arrays.copyOf(a,n),new int[]{1,2,3});

Random random=new Random(42);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[random.nextInt(16)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=random.nextInt(8)-4;Arrays.sort(a);int[] b=a.clone(),c=a.clone();int expected=uniqueBrute(b);assert uniqueWithList(c)==expected;assert unique(a)==expected;assert Arrays.equals(Arrays.copyOf(a,expected),Arrays.copyOf(b,expected));assert Arrays.equals(Arrays.copyOf(c,expected),Arrays.copyOf(b,expected));}

better.explanation: Sorted duplicates sit together. Add a number to the temporary list only when it differs from its previous neighbour.

reference.title: remove-duplicates lesson
reference.approach: a temporary list, adjacent comparisons, then two pointers

43.problem: Rotate an array one position to the left in place.
43.assumptions: The first element moves to the end. An empty array stays empty.

example.explanation: Save 1, shift 2, 3 and 4 one position left, then place the saved 1 in the last slot.

43.baseline: Create a second array and write each value at its shifted index, using O(n) space.
43.approach:
The first value is the only one that will be lost when you shift left. Save it before moving anything.

Copy each later value into the position just before it. Once those moves finish, put the saved value in the final position.
steps: Handle empty input.
Save the original first element.
Shift the remaining elements left and fill the final slot.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite the first element before saving it.
A single-element array remains unchanged.
tests: int[] a={1,2,3,4}; rotateOne(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{2,3,4,1});

reference.title: left-rotation lesson
reference.approach: the one-place shift used by its repeated-rotation approach
reference.adaptation: This tracker question asks for one position, so the code performs that shift once.

44.problem: Rotate an array d positions to the left in place.
44.assumptions: d is nonnegative. Rotations wrap around; d is reduced modulo the array length.

example.explanation: Move the first block [2, 4] after the other block [6, 8, 10, 12]. The table shows how three reversals do that.

44.baseline: Repeat a one-place left shift d times. First reduce d modulo n so complete turns are skipped.
44.approach:
Split the array after the first d numbers. Reverse each block, then reverse the whole array.

The last reversal exchanges the blocks. It also reverses each block a second time, restoring the order of the numbers inside it.
steps: Return for an empty or single-element array.
Reduce d modulo the length. Return if it becomes zero.
Reverse the first block, the second block, then the entire array.
pitfalls: Do not compute d % n for n=0.
A right rotation uses a different split; make the direction explicit.
tests: int[] a={1,2,3,4,5}; rotate(a,2); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{3,4,5,1,2});
int[] b={1,2,3}; rotate(b,6); assert Arrays.equals(b,new int[]{1,2,3});

Random random=new Random(44);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[random.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=random.nextInt();int d=random.nextInt(30);int[] b=a.clone(),c=a.clone();rotateRepeated(b,d);rotateWithBuffer(c,d);rotate(a,d);assert Arrays.equals(a,b);assert Arrays.equals(a,c);}
44.baselineTime: O(n × (d % n)) for nonempty input, with O(1) extra space.

better.explanation: Save the first d numbers. Shift the rest left by d, then copy the saved numbers to the end.

reference.title: left-rotation lesson
reference.approach: repeated shifts, a temporary block, then three reversals

45.problem: Move all zeroes to the end while preserving the relative order of nonzero values.
45.assumptions: The array is modified in place.

example.explanation: Keep the order 4, -2, 7. Each one takes the next available place at the front; zeros move behind them.

45.baseline: Collect nonzero values in a temporary array, followed by zeros. Copy the result back.
45.approach:
write marks the next place for a nonzero number. Scan from left to right. When you see a nonzero number, swap it into that place and move write forward.

Before the first zero, these are harmless swaps with the same position. After a zero, each swap moves a useful number left and a zero right.
steps: Start write at zero.
Skip zeros; swap each nonzero value with nums[write].
Advance write only after placing a nonzero value.
pitfalls: Do not sort: that changes the order of the nonzero numbers.
Advance write only for nonzero values.
Both in-place methods take O(n) time. Swapping combines the work into one scan.
tests: int[] a={0,1,0,3,12}; moveZeroes(a); assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,3,12,0,0});
int[] b={0,0}; moveZeroes(b); assert Arrays.equals(b,new int[]{0,0});

Random random=new Random(45);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[random.nextInt(15)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=random.nextInt(5)-2;int[] b=a.clone(),c=a.clone();moveZeroesBuffer(b);moveZeroesFill(c);moveZeroes(a);assert Arrays.equals(a,b);assert Arrays.equals(a,c);}

better.explanation: Copy nonzero values into the front of the same array. After the scan, fill every remaining position with zero.

reference.title: move-zeroes lesson
reference.approach: a helper array, in-place copying, then two-pointer swaps

46.problem: Find the first index at which a target value appears in an array.
46.assumptions: The input need not be sorted. Return -1 when the target is absent.

example.explanation: The first value matches, so the search stops before visiting the remaining elements.

46.baseline: Checking every position is already the appropriate baseline for one search in arbitrary unsorted data.
46.approach:
Imagine checking a row of numbered boxes. Open them from left to right and stop at the first matching number.

If the array is unsorted, a skipped box could contain the answer. A missing target therefore makes you check every box.
steps: Compare each element with the target.
Return its index on the first equality.
Return -1 only after the scan finishes.
46.time: O(n) worst case, O(1) best case.
pitfalls: Returning zero for absence confuses not-found with a match at index zero.
Binary search cannot replace this scan unless the ordering assumptions hold.

reference.title: linear-search lesson
reference.approach: checking left to right and returning the first match

47.problem: Return the sorted union of two sorted arrays, including each distinct value once.
47.assumptions: Both arrays are ascending and may contain duplicates.

example.explanation: Merge their next values in order, but append only when the chosen value differs from the last output value.

47.baseline: Insert everything into a TreeSet, costing O((n+m) log(n+m)) time.
47.approach: Two pointers exploit existing order. Each step consumes one smallest remaining value; a last-output check removes duplicates from either source.
steps: Choose the smaller current head, or the only remaining head.
Advance that array’s pointer.
Append only when the output is empty or its last value differs.
47.space: O(u) for u output values; O(1) auxiliary state beyond the result.
pitfalls: A union is not concatenation and does not retain duplicate multiplicities.
Do not read a head after that input has been exhausted.

48.problem: Find the one missing value from the range 1 through n.
48.assumptions: The array contains n−1 distinct values from that range. This is the 1-based variant; some platforms instead use 0 through n.

example.explanation: XOR all numbers 1 through 5, then XOR the supplied values. Every present number cancels with itself, leaving 3.

48.baseline: Use a presence array to mark values, requiring O(n) extra storage.
48.approach: XOR is associative and commutative, x XOR x is zero, and x XOR zero is x. Cancellation removes every paired value without arithmetic-sum overflow.
steps: Infer n as array length plus one.
XOR all expected values.
XOR all supplied values and return the remainder.
pitfalls: Duplicates or out-of-range values violate the premise and invalidate cancellation.
For the 0-based variant, XOR indices 0 through length−1 and the final length instead.

49.problem: Find the longest contiguous run of ones in a binary array.
49.assumptions: Values are zero or one. Empty input returns zero.

example.explanation: The first run has length two. Zero resets the current count; the final run reaches three.

49.baseline: Start a new scan at every one and count its run, repeating work and taking O(n²) in the worst case.
49.approach: The only state needed is the length of the run ending at the current position and the best completed-or-current run.
steps: Increment current when the value is one.
Reset current on zero.
Update best after each element.
pitfalls: Do not reset the overall best when a zero appears.
Remember to count a run that reaches the final element.

50.problem: Find the value that appears once when every other value appears exactly twice.
50.assumptions: The input is nonempty and satisfies the stated multiplicities. Negative values are allowed.

example.explanation: Both ones cancel under XOR, as do both twos. Only 4 remains.

50.baseline: Count frequencies in a map and find the key with count one, using O(n) additional space.
50.approach: XOR cancellation does not depend on order. Scanning once with a zero accumulator removes every duplicated pair.
steps: Initialize the accumulator to zero.
XOR in every value.
Return the final accumulator.
pitfalls: This does not solve the variant where other values appear three times.
The technique assumes the multiplicity promise; it does not validate it.

51.problem: Find the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose sum equals k.
51.assumptions: This sliding-window version requires nonnegative elements and k>=0. Empty subarrays do not contribute positive length.

example.explanation: The first window [1,2] has length two. Later the window [1,1,1] also sums to three and has length three.

51.baseline: Enumerate all subarray boundaries and accumulate sums, taking O(n²) time.
51.approach: With nonnegative values, extending right never lowers the sum and removing left never raises it. When the sum is too large, shrinking from the left cannot discard a valid longer window ending at the same right position.
steps: Add the next rightmost value.
While the sum exceeds k, remove leftmost values.
When equal, compare the current window length with the best.
51.time: O(n): each index enters and leaves the window at most once.
pitfalls: Negative numbers destroy the monotonic-sum property; use prefix sums for that variant.
Zeroes are supported and can extend a valid window without changing its sum.
Use long for the running sum.

52.problem: Find the longest contiguous subarray with sum k when values may be positive, zero, or negative.
52.assumptions: Return zero if no nonempty matching subarray exists.

example.explanation: The first four values sum to three. A prefix sum of three at index 3 pairs with the initial zero prefix at index -1, producing length 4.

52.baseline: Compute every subarray sum in O(n²) time using a running sum for each start.
52.approach: A subarray ending at i sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals prefix[i]−k. Keep the earliest index for each prefix, because it yields the longest matching interval.
steps: Seed prefix zero at index −1.
Update the running sum and look up sum−k.
Record a prefix only on its first occurrence.
pitfalls: Overwriting an earlier prefix index can shorten the reported answer.
A sliding window is not generally valid with negative values.
tests: Random r=new Random(52); for(int run=0;run<200;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(12)]; for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(9)-4; int k=r.nextInt(11)-5,best=0; for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){long sum=0;for(int j=i;j<a.length;j++){sum+=a[j];if(sum==k)best=Math.max(best,j-i+1);}} assert longestSum(a,k)==best;}

53.problem: Return two different indices whose values add to a target.
53.assumptions: Return an empty array if no pair exists; any valid pair is acceptable.

example.explanation: After remembering 2 at index 0, the value 7 asks for complement 2 and finds it.

53.baseline: Try every pair of distinct indices in O(n²) time.
53.approach: Store earlier values in a hash map. Looking up the complement before inserting the current value prevents an element from pairing with itself.
steps: Scan indices from left to right.
Look for target minus the current value among earlier values.
Return the two indices on a match; otherwise remember the current value.
pitfalls: Use long for the complement when int subtraction might overflow.
Two equal values can form a pair only if they occupy different indices.

54.problem: Sort an array containing only zeroes, ones, and twos in place.
54.assumptions: The three-value domain is a precondition.

example.explanation: A zero belongs in the left region, a two in the right region, and a one stays in the middle.

54.baseline: Count each value and overwrite the array in two passes; this is also O(n) time and O(1) space.
54.approach: The Dutch national flag partition maintains zeroes before low, ones from low to mid−1, unknown values from mid to high, and twos after high. Every iteration shrinks the unknown region.
steps: For zero, swap with low and advance both low and mid.
For one, advance mid.
For two, swap with high and decrement high; inspect the incoming mid value again.
pitfalls: Advancing mid after swapping a two can skip an unclassified value.
This implementation assumes valid input; it treats any other value like two.
tests: Random r=new Random(54);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(30)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(3);int[] b=a.clone();Arrays.sort(b);sortColors(a);assert Arrays.equals(a,b);}

55.problem: Find a value appearing more than half the time, if one exists.
55.assumptions: The result is OptionalInt.empty when no strict majority exists.

example.explanation: Cancelling unlike pairs leaves 2 as the candidate. A second pass counts four copies, exceeding 7/2.

55.baseline: Count frequencies in a hash map using O(n) space.
55.approach: Boyer–Moore voting cancels pairs of different values. Removing such a pair cannot eliminate a strict majority from the remaining multiset. The survivor is only a candidate unless existence is guaranteed.
steps: Choose a new candidate whenever balance becomes zero.
Increase balance for a match and decrease it otherwise.
Verify that the final candidate occurs more than n/2 times.
pitfalls: A surviving candidate does not prove that a majority exists.
The threshold is strictly greater than half, not greater than or equal.

56.problem: Return the maximum sum among nonempty contiguous subarrays.
56.assumptions: The array is nonempty. Negative numbers are allowed; the empty subarray is excluded.

example.explanation: The best segment is [4,-1,2,1]. Its sum is 6; carrying the earlier negative prefix into it would only reduce that sum.

56.baseline: Enumerate starts and ends with running sums in O(n²) time.
56.approach: Kadane’s recurrence says the best subarray ending here either starts here or extends the best subarray ending immediately before. If that previous sum is negative, starting afresh is better.
steps: Initialize ending and best from the first element.
Set ending to max(current, ending + current).
Update the overall best after each position.
pitfalls: Initializing best to zero wrongly accepts the empty subarray on all-negative input.
Use long when many int values can accumulate.
tests: Random r=new Random(56);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(21)-10;long best=Long.MIN_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){long s=0;for(int j=i;j<a.length;j++){s+=a[j];best=Math.max(best,s);}}assert maxSum(a)==best;}

57.problem: Return the boundaries of a maximum-sum nonempty subarray.
57.assumptions: The returned pair is [startInclusive, endExclusive]. Ties may return any maximizing segment.

example.explanation: At index 3, extending the previous negative sum loses to starting at 4. The running segment then reaches sum 6 at index 6.

57.baseline: Enumerate every interval and remember the best boundaries in O(n²) time.
57.approach: Extend Kadane’s algorithm with a candidate start. Whenever the best sum ending here restarts, move that start to the current index. Copy both boundaries only when the overall best improves.
steps: Track the start of the current candidate.
Restart when the previous ending sum is negative.
On a new best, save candidate start and current index plus one.
57.space: O(1); copying the selected segment separately costs O(length).
pitfalls: Do not update the saved answer boundaries when only the current candidate changes.
Be explicit about inclusive versus exclusive end indices.

58.problem: Maximize profit from at most one purchase followed by one sale.
58.assumptions: Prices are nonnegative. Buying must precede selling; choosing no trade gives profit zero.

example.explanation: Buy at 1 and sell later at 6. The earlier price 7 is not a valid selling price for that purchase.

58.baseline: Try all buy/sell index pairs in O(n²) time.
58.approach: For each potential sale, the cheapest earlier price is the best purchase. Maintain that minimum as the scan advances.
steps: Keep the minimum price seen so far.
Compare the current sale profit with the best.
Update the minimum for later sales.
pitfalls: The global minimum and maximum are insufficient if the maximum occurs first.
This is one transaction, not the unlimited-transactions variant.

59.problem: Alternate positive and negative values while retaining their relative order within each sign.
59.assumptions: There are equally many positive and negative values, no zeroes, and the output starts positive.

example.explanation: The positives 3,1,2 fill even positions in order. The negatives -2,-5,-4 fill odd positions.

59.baseline: Separate the signs into two lists and interleave them, also taking O(n) extra space.
59.approach: Two output cursors, one even and one odd, encode the required arrangement directly. Scanning in original order preserves stability.
steps: Allocate an output array of the same length.
Write positives at 0,2,4,… and negatives at 1,3,5,… .
Reject zeroes or unbalanced signs for this particular variant.
pitfalls: Unequal sign counts require a different contract, such as appending leftovers.
Swapping signs in place generally loses stable ordering.

60.problem: Replace a permutation with the next lexicographically larger permutation in place.
60.assumptions: Repeated values are allowed. If the input is already greatest, return it to ascending order.

example.explanation: The suffix [3,2] is descending. Increase pivot 1 to the smallest larger suffix value, 2, then reverse the remaining suffix to obtain its smallest order.

60.baseline: Generate all distinct permutations and choose the next, which takes factorial time.
60.approach: A descending suffix is already its largest arrangement. Therefore the rightmost position that can increase is just before that suffix. The rightmost larger suffix element gives the smallest possible increase; reversing the resulting descending suffix minimizes the tail.
steps: Find the rightmost index i with a[i] < a[i+1].
If it exists, swap with the rightmost value greater than a[i].
Reverse the suffix after i; if no pivot exists, reverse the entire array.
pitfalls: The pivot comparison must be strict so duplicates do not create a false increase.
Choose the rightmost larger value, not the largest value.

61.problem: Return elements strictly greater than every element to their right.
61.assumptions: This explanation uses strict leaders; some platforms allow equality. Return leaders in original order.

example.explanation: The rightmost 6 leads. Scanning left, 12 exceeds 6 and 22 exceeds 12; all other values fail.

61.baseline: Compare each element with its entire suffix in O(n²) time.
61.approach: A right-to-left scan keeps the maximum of the suffix already visited. The current element is a leader exactly when it exceeds that maximum.
steps: Scan from the final index backward.
Append a value if it is greater than the suffix maximum.
Reverse the collected leaders to restore original order.
61.space: O(k) for k returned leaders; O(1) additional state.
pitfalls: Using >= changes the treatment of duplicate maximum values.
A sentinel outside the int domain allows Integer.MIN_VALUE to be a leader.

62.problem: Find the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integer values present in an unsorted array.
62.assumptions: The values need not be adjacent in the array. Duplicates do not extend a sequence.

example.explanation: The values 1,2,3,4 form one sequence even though they appear out of order.

62.baseline: Sort a copy and scan distinct neighboring values in O(n log n) time.
62.approach: Use a set and start a forward walk only at a value whose predecessor is absent. Each distinct value belongs to exactly one such walk, preventing repeated scans of the same sequence.
steps: Build a set of distinct values.
Skip values with an existing predecessor.
Walk successors from each true start and keep the longest length.
62.time: Expected O(n): each distinct value is walked once.
pitfalls: Starting a walk from every value can degrade to O(n²).
Guard predecessor/successor arithmetic at integer boundaries to prevent wraparound.

63.problem: If an original matrix cell is zero, set its entire row and column to zero.
63.assumptions: The matrix is rectangular and may be empty. Modify it in place.

example.explanation: The original zero marks row 1 and column 1. Their intersection with other rows and columns is cleared; newly written zeroes must not create more markers.

63.baseline: Record affected rows and columns in separate boolean arrays, using O(rows+columns) space.
63.approach: Reuse the first row and first column as markers. Preserve whether those two borders originally contained zeroes in separate flags, because the shared corner cannot encode both independently.
steps: Remember whether the first row or first column originally has a zero.
Scan the interior and mark its affected borders.
Clear interior cells using those markers, then clear the flagged borders.
pitfalls: Clearing rows immediately can treat newly created zeroes as original zeroes.
Process the border flags last so markers remain available.

64.problem: Rotate a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place.
64.assumptions: The matrix is n×n. A rectangular matrix needs a differently shaped output.

example.explanation: Transposing turns columns into rows. Reversing each transposed row makes the original bottom-left 7 become the new top-left.

64.baseline: Write each old cell (r,c) into a new matrix at (c,n−1−r), using O(n²) space.
64.approach: Transposition maps (r,c) to (c,r); row reversal then maps it to (c,n−1−r), exactly the clockwise rotation mapping.
steps: Transpose by swapping only entries above the diagonal.
Reverse every row.
Keep diagonal entries untouched during transposition.
pitfalls: Swapping both halves of the diagonal undoes the transpose.
Reversing rows before transposing produces the opposite rotation.

65.problem: Read a rectangular matrix in clockwise spiral order, starting at the top-left.
65.assumptions: Return an empty list for an empty matrix.

example.explanation: Visit the top edge, right edge, bottom edge backward, and left edge upward, then repeat on the remaining inner rectangle.

65.baseline: Track a visited grid and turn direction whenever the next cell is blocked, using O(rows×columns) extra state.
65.approach: Four boundaries describe all unvisited cells. Consuming an edge moves its boundary inward. Rechecking the boundaries before the last two edges prevents duplicates in one-row or one-column remainders.
steps: Traverse top, then increment top.
Traverse right, then decrement right.
If rows remain, traverse bottom backward; if columns remain, traverse left upward.
pitfalls: Without the boundary rechecks, the middle row or column may be visited twice.
Java permits ragged arrays, but this contract requires a rectangle.

66.problem: Count nonempty contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.
66.assumptions: Values can be positive, negative, or zero. Return a long because the count can be quadratic.

example.explanation: The intervals at indices [0,1] and [1,2] both sum to 2. They correspond to two different matching pairs of prefix sums.

66.baseline: Enumerate all starts and ends in O(n²) time.
66.approach: For the current prefix sum s, every earlier prefix equal to s−k defines one matching subarray. A frequency map counts all such starts, including repeated identical prefix sums.
steps: Seed prefix zero with frequency one.
Add the current value, then add the frequency of sum−k to the answer.
Increment the frequency of the current sum after querying.
pitfalls: Querying after insertion incorrectly counts an empty subarray when k=0.
Store frequencies, not merely membership: different starts can share a prefix sum.

67.problem: Build the first n rows of Pascal’s triangle. Every row starts and ends with 1. Each inside number is the sum of the two numbers above it.
67.assumptions: Striver’s first-N-rows lesson allows 1 to 30 rows. These values fit in int. This method also returns an empty list for zero rows.

example.explanation: To build the fourth row, keep 1 at each end. Its two middle values are 1 + 2 = 3 and 2 + 1 = 3.

67.baseline: Calculate each cell recursively from its two parents. This repeatedly calculates the same earlier cells.
67.baselineTime: O(2ⁿ) across the triangle; O(n) recursion depth, plus the output.
67.approach:
The previous row is already in the answer. Read its numbers instead of calculating them again.

Begin the new row with 1s. Leave the ends alone and replace each inside entry with the sum of its two parents.
steps: Make a new list for each row. Row 0 has one entry, row 1 has two, and so on.
Fill columns 1 through row - 1 using the previous row.
Add the finished row to the triangle.
67.time: O(n²): that many numbers must be written.
67.space: O(n²) for the returned rows; O(1) beyond those rows.
pitfalls: Create a fresh list for each row. Reusing one list changes earlier rows too.
The int version relies on the row limit; it is not suitable for arbitrarily large triangles.

reference.title: Pascal’s triangle
reference.approach: recursive cells, then building rows from the previous row

tests: List<List<Integer>> rows=pascal(30);for(int i=0;i<rows.size();i++){long sum=0;for(int x:rows.get(i))sum+=x;assert sum==(1L<<i);assert rows.get(i).size()==i+1;for(int j=0;j<=i;j++)assert rows.get(i).get(j).equals(rows.get(i).get(i-j));}

68.problem: Find every value appearing strictly more than n/3 times.
68.assumptions: At most two distinct values can satisfy the threshold. Output order is unspecified.

example.explanation: Both 1 and 2 occur three times, which exceeds 7/3. A third qualifying value would require more than seven total positions.

68.baseline: Count frequencies in a map in O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
68.approach: Generalized voting maintains two candidates. When a value matches neither occupied slot, decrement both balances: this cancels a group of three distinct values. Every true n/3 majority survives as a candidate, but both candidates still require verification.
steps: Match existing candidates before replacing an empty slot.
When both slots are occupied by other values, decrement both counts.
Count actual occurrences of both survivors and apply the strict threshold.
68.space: O(1), including at most two output values.
pitfalls: Verify candidates; voting balances are not occurrence counts.
Check matches before empty slots to avoid assigning both slots the same value.
tests: Random r=new Random(68);for(int run=0;run<200;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];Map<Integer,Integer> counts=new HashMap<>();for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){a[i]=r.nextInt(7)-3;counts.merge(a[i],1,Integer::sum);}Set<Integer> expected=new HashSet<>();for(var e:counts.entrySet())if(e.getValue()>a.length/3)expected.add(e.getKey());assert new HashSet<>(majorities(a)).equals(expected);}

69.problem: Return all unique triples of values whose sum is zero.
69.assumptions: The same index cannot be used twice. The input is sorted in place; duplicate value triples appear only once.

example.explanation: After sorting, fixing the first -1 leaves a two-pointer search that finds both (-1,2) and (0,1). Repeating the same fixed value would duplicate those triples.

69.baseline: Enumerate index triples in O(n³) time and deduplicate their values.
69.approach: Sort first. With one fixed value, increasing the left pointer raises the sum and decreasing the right pointer lowers it. This monotonicity lets one scan replace a nested pair enumeration.
steps: Skip duplicate fixed values.
Use left and right pointers on the remaining suffix.
After a match, skip repeated values at both pointers.
69.time: O(n²), dominated by the two-pointer scans.
69.space: O(log n) sorting stack plus O(k) returned triples.
pitfalls: Use long before adding int values to avoid overflow.
Sorting changes original indices; this version returns values.

70.problem: Return unique quadruples of values whose sum equals a target.
70.assumptions: Use four different indices. The array is sorted in place; target is long.

example.explanation: Fixing -2 and -1 leaves target 3 for the two remaining pointers, which find 1 and 2. Other fixed pairs yield the remaining distinct quadruples.

70.baseline: Enumerate four indices in O(n⁴) time and deduplicate results.
70.approach: Fix the first two values in sorted order, then solve the remaining pair with converging pointers. Duplicate skipping is needed independently at both fixed positions and after each matching pair.
steps: Sort and loop over the first two indices.
Skip repeated fixed values at the same depth.
Move the remaining pointers according to the long sum and skip duplicate matches.
70.space: O(log n) sorting stack plus returned output.
pitfalls: Casting after an overflowing int sum is too late; cast the first operand.
For the second fixed index, skip duplicates only when j > i+1.

71.problem: Find the length of the longest zero-sum contiguous subarray.
71.assumptions: Values may have either sign; return zero if no nonempty zero-sum interval exists.

example.explanation: The segment [-2,2,-8,1,7] sums to zero. Prefix sum 15 occurs at indices 0 and 5, so the intervening five values cancel.

71.baseline: Enumerate all intervals in O(n²) time.
71.approach: Equal prefix sums delimit a zero-sum interval. Remember the earliest index of each sum so every later repetition gives the longest possible interval for that endpoint.
steps: Seed sum zero at index −1.
Accumulate each value using long.
On a repeated sum, measure distance from its first occurrence.
pitfalls: Keeping the latest prefix index loses longer intervals.
The initial zero prefix makes an interval starting at index zero count correctly.

72.problem: Count nonempty contiguous subarrays whose bitwise XOR equals k.
72.assumptions: Input and k are int values. Use long for the number of intervals.

example.explanation: The matching segments are [4,2], [4,2,2,6,4], [2,2,6], and [6].

72.baseline: Enumerate every start and extend its XOR in O(n²) time.
72.approach: If current prefix XOR is x and earlier prefix XOR is p, the interval XOR is x XOR p. Requiring k gives p = x XOR k. Count all earlier prefixes with that value.
steps: Seed XOR zero with frequency one.
Update the current prefix XOR.
Add the frequency of prefix XOR k, then record the current prefix.
pitfalls: XOR cancellation uses XOR, not subtraction.
Query before insertion to avoid counting empty intervals when k=0.

73.problem: Merge overlapping closed intervals and return disjoint intervals in sorted order.
73.assumptions: Each interval is [start,end] with start<=end. Touching intervals overlap because endpoints are included. The input row order is changed by sorting.

example.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, extending the current end to 6. The next interval starts after 6, so it begins a new group.

73.baseline: Repeatedly merge any intersecting pair until none remain; naive rescanning can take quadratic or worse time.
73.approach: Sorting by start means a new interval can overlap only the last merged interval. Earlier merged intervals already end before it. Extend the last end or append a new interval.
steps: Sort by start with Integer.compare.
Append the first interval as a new output array.
For each later interval, merge if its start is at most the last end.
73.space: O(n) including output and object-array sorting workspace.
pitfalls: Using subtraction in a comparator can overflow.
Use < instead of <= for overlap only if the problem defines non-touching or half-open intervals.

74.problem: Merge two sorted arrays using their existing storage.
74.assumptions: Afterward the first array contains the smallest n values and the second contains the largest m values, both sorted. Neither array has spare capacity.

example.explanation: Treat both arrays as one virtual sequence. Compare values separated by shrinking gaps, swapping inversions even when the pair crosses the array boundary.

74.baseline: Merge into an auxiliary array and copy back in O(n+m) time but O(n+m) space. Inserting each out-of-place value across the boundary needs no extra space but may take O(nm) time.
74.approach: The gap method progressively moves misplaced values across the two initially sorted runs. Start with ceil((n+m)/2), compare every pair at that distance, and repeatedly halve upward until a final gap-one pass. The two-sorted-runs precondition is essential; this is not a general one-pass-per-gap sorting algorithm.
steps: Access index i in a when i<n, otherwise in b at i−n.
At each gap, swap inverted pairs while scanning left to right.
After processing gap one, stop.
pitfalls: Do not round the gap down in a way that skips required comparisons.
The variant with spare slots at the end of the first array instead supports a simpler O(n+m) backward merge.
tests: int[] a={1,4,8,10},b={2,3,9};merge(a,b);assert Arrays.equals(a,new int[]{1,2,3,4});assert Arrays.equals(b,new int[]{8,9,10});

Random r=new Random(74);for(int run=0;run<500;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)],b=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(41)-20;for(int i=0;i<b.length;i++)b[i]=r.nextInt(41)-20;Arrays.sort(a);Arrays.sort(b);int[] all=new int[a.length+b.length];System.arraycopy(a,0,all,0,a.length);System.arraycopy(b,0,all,a.length,b.length);Arrays.sort(all);merge(a,b);assert Arrays.equals(a,Arrays.copyOfRange(all,0,a.length));assert Arrays.equals(b,Arrays.copyOfRange(all,a.length,all.length));}

75.problem: Find the repeated and missing values in an array intended to contain 1 through n.
75.assumptions: Exactly one value appears twice and exactly one value is absent; all others appear once. Return [repeated,missing].

example.explanation: XORing the array with 1 through 5 leaves 3 XOR 4. A bit on which 3 and 4 differ separates them into two groups; a final scan identifies 3 as the repeated value.

75.baseline: Use a frequency array of n+1 entries, costing O(n) space.
75.approach: All correct pairs cancel under XOR, leaving the XOR of the two exceptional values. Its lowest set bit partitions all values into two groups, each containing exactly one exception. XOR within each group isolates them without square-sum overflow.
steps: XOR actual and expected values to obtain the exceptional XOR.
Split both sets by one set bit and XOR each group.
Check which recovered value appears in the input.
pitfalls: The XOR result alone does not identify which value is missing versus repeated.
