This relies on the promised multiplicities and range; malformed input needs separate validation.
tests: for(int n=2;n<15;n++)for(int missing=1;missing<=n;missing++)for(int repeated=1;repeated<=n;repeated++){if(missing==repeated)continue;int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=i+1==missing?repeated:i+1;assert Arrays.equals(repeatedMissing(a),new int[]{repeated,missing});}

76.assumptions: Equal values do not form inversions. The method sorts the input as a side effect and returns long.

example.explanation: The leading 5 contributes four inversions, 3 contributes two, 2 contributes one, and 4 contributes one.

76.baseline: Compare every ordered index pair in O(n²) time.
76.approach: During merge sort, both halves are already sorted. If the next right value is smaller than the next left value, it is smaller than every remaining left value, adding all those cross inversions at once.
steps: Recursively count inversions within each half.
Merge the halves into a reusable buffer.
When taking a strictly smaller right value, add the number of unmerged left values.
76.space: O(n) buffer plus O(log n) recursion.
pitfalls: Use <= when selecting the left value so equal pairs are not counted.
The maximum n(n−1)/2 can exceed int.
tests: Random r=new Random(76);for(int run=0;run<200;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(21)-10;long expected=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<a.length;j++)if(a[i]>a[j])expected++;assert inversions(a)==expected;}

77.assumptions: Values can be negative. The input is sorted as a side effect; return a long count.

example.explanation: The 3 at index 1 and the 3 at index 3 each form a pair with the final 1. Equality, such as 2 versus 2×1, does not count.

77.baseline: Test every index pair in O(n²) time.
77.approach: Merge sort separates pairs inside each half from cross pairs. For sorted halves, a right prefix satisfies the inequality for a fixed left value. As left values increase, that right prefix can only grow, so one pointer counts all cross pairs linearly.
steps: Count recursively within both halves.
Before merging, advance a right pointer while the doubled-value inequality holds.
Add its distance from the right-half start for each left value, then merge normally.
pitfalls: Count cross pairs before the ordinary merge destroys the half boundary.
Use 2L*a[j]; int multiplication can overflow and reverse the comparison.
Negative equal values can satisfy the condition, for example -3 > 2×-3.
tests: Random r=new Random(77);for(int run=0;run<200;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;long expected=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<a.length;j++)if((long)a[i]>2L*a[j])expected++;assert reversePairs(a)==expected;}

78.problem: Find the largest product you can make by multiplying a nonempty run of neighbouring numbers.
78.assumptions: Return 0 for an empty array, as in the linked lesson. The long implementation assumes every intermediate product fits in long.

example.explanation: After reading 2, the smallest product ending there is -6. Multiplying that by -4 gives 24. Keeping only the largest product would miss this answer.

78.baseline: Choose every start and end. Multiply the numbers in each selected range from scratch.

better.explanation: For each start, extend the end one place at a time. Multiply only the newly included number.

78.approach:
A negative number can turn a very small product into a very large one. Remember both the smallest and largest products ending at the previous position.

At the next number, either start again there or extend one of those two products. Choose the smallest and largest of the three results.
steps: Set both ending products and the overall answer to the first number.
Save both old products before updating either one.
Calculate the new minimum and maximum. Compare the maximum with the overall answer.
pitfalls: Do not initialise the answer to 0: a single negative number must return itself.
Use the old minimum and maximum for both calculations.
Zero needs no special reset: starting at the current number is already an option.

reference.title: maximum product subarray
reference.approach: all ranges, reused running products, then minimum/maximum ending products

tests: assert maxProduct(new int[]{-2,0,-1})==0;assert maxProduct(new int[]{-7})==-7;assert maxProduct(new int[]{})==0;

Random random=new Random(78);for(int t=0;t<300;t++){int[] a=new int[random.nextInt(9)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=random.nextInt(7)-3;long expected=maxProductBrute(a);assert maxProduct(a)==expected;assert maxProductBetter(a)==expected;}

80.problem: Find the first position where the value is at least the target. The target itself does not have to be in the array.
80.assumptions: The array is sorted. If no value is large enough, return the array length.

example.explanation: Indices 1, 2 and 3 all contain 2. We need the first one, so finding a matching 2 is a reason to look farther left.

80.baseline: Read from left to right. Return as soon as a value is at least the target. If you reach the end, return the array length.
80.approach:
Finding a value that works is only half the job: you need the earliest one. Save its index in answer, then look to its left. If you find an earlier valid index, replace answer.

When the middle value is too small, everything before it is too small too. Move low past the middle. Start answer at the array length so the no-answer case is already covered.
steps: Start low at 0, high at the final index, and answer at the array length.
If arr[mid] >= target, remember mid and set high to mid - 1.
Otherwise, set low to mid + 1.
When the search ends, return the last saved answer.
80.time: O(log n): each check removes about half the remaining positions.
80.space: O(1): a few index variables, with no extra array.
pitfalls: Do not return immediately on equality; another equal value may appear earlier.
The result may equal the array length. That is a valid result, but it is not a valid index to read.
Keep >= here. Changing it to > solves upper bound instead.
tests: Random random=new Random(80);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[] arr=new int[random.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<arr.length;i++)arr[i]=random.nextInt(11)-5;Arrays.sort(arr);for(int target=-6;target<=6;target++)assert lowerBound(arr,target)==lowerBoundLinear(arr,target);}
80.baselineTime: O(n): you may need to inspect every element.

reference.title: lower bound
reference.approach: binary search with a saved answer, continuing left after a valid candidate

81.problem: Find the first position whose value is larger than the target. Equal values do not count.
81.assumptions: The array is sorted. If all values are smaller than or equal to the target, return the array length.

example.explanation: Skip every 2. The first larger value is 4, which is at index 4.

81.baseline: Scan from the left and return the first index whose value is larger than the target. Return the array length if you find none.
81.approach:
This is almost the same search as lower bound. The difference is what you do with equality: a 2 is not an answer when you need something larger than 2, so keep looking right.

When you find a larger value, save its index and search left. There may be an earlier value that is also large enough. The saved answer lets you keep searching without losing a valid result.
steps: Set answer to the array length and search between low = 0 and high = n - 1.
If arr[mid] > target, save mid and move high to mid - 1.
If arr[mid] <= target, move low to mid + 1.
Return answer after low passes high.
81.time: O(log n): each check removes about half the remaining positions.
81.space: O(1): a few index variables, with no extra array.
pitfalls: Use > when checking a candidate. >= would include equal values and give lower bound.
Avoid computing target + 1 to reuse another search; it overflows at Integer.MAX_VALUE.
Returning n is expected when the target is at least the largest element.
tests: Random random=new Random(81);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[] arr=new int[random.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<arr.length;i++)arr[i]=random.nextInt(11)-5;Arrays.sort(arr);for(int target=-6;target<=6;target++)assert upperBound(arr,target)==upperBoundLinear(arr,target);}
81.baselineTime: O(n): you may need to inspect every element.

reference.title: upper bound
reference.approach: binary search with a saved answer, continuing left after a valid candidate

rows: Equal is not enough. Move low to 3.

82.problem: Find where a target should be inserted to keep an array sorted.
82.assumptions: Return the first occurrence when the target already exists. Insertion is conceptual; the array is not resized.

example.explanation: 7 belongs between 5 and 8. The first value at least 7 is 8, at index 2.

82.baseline: Scan for the first value not smaller than the target in O(n) time.
82.approach:
Look for the first value that is at least the target. If it equals the target, you have found its first position. If it is larger, the target belongs just before it.

Save each suitable midpoint, then check to its left for an earlier position. If every value is too small, the target belongs at the end.
steps: Start answer at the array length.
When arr[mid] is at least the target, save mid and move high left.
Otherwise move low right. Return the saved answer when the search ends.
pitfalls: An answer equal to n is valid, even though reading a[n] is not.
Returning any matching duplicate is insufficient if insertion must precede equal values.
tests: Random r=new Random(82);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(21)-10;Arrays.sort(a);int target=r.nextInt(25)-12;assert insertPosition(a,target)==insertLinear(a,target);}

reference.title: search-insert-position
reference.approach: a linear scan, then lower bound with a saved answer

83.problem: Find the greatest value <=x and the smallest value >=x in a sorted array.
83.assumptions: The input is sorted and contains positive values, as in the current Striver problem. Return [floor value, ceiling value], using -1 for a missing side.

example.explanation: The first value >=3 is 4. Since it is not equal to 3, its predecessor 2 is the floor.

83.baseline: Read every number. Keep the largest one no greater than x and the smallest one no smaller than x.
83.approach:
For the floor, a number no greater than x is a possible answer. Save it and look right for a larger one that still fits.

For the ceiling, a number no smaller than x is a possible answer. Save it and look left for a smaller one that still fits. An exact match can serve as both.
steps: Search for the floor, moving right after saving a valid value.
Search for the ceiling, moving left after saving a valid value.
Return the two values; a side that never found a candidate stays -1.
pitfalls: Return values, not indices, for the combined problem.
Use <= for the floor and >= for the ceiling: an exact match belongs to both.
The -1 convention relies on the problem’s positive-value inputs.
tests: assert Arrays.equals(floorCeil(new int[]{3,5},1),new int[]{-1,3});assert Arrays.equals(floorCeil(new int[]{3,5},9),new int[]{5,-1});
assert Arrays.equals(floorCeil(new int[]{1,2},2),new int[]{2,2});assert Arrays.equals(floorCeil(new int[]{},2),new int[]{-1,-1});

Random r=new Random(83);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(20)+1;Arrays.sort(a);int target=r.nextInt(22)+1;assert Arrays.equals(floorCeil(a,target),floorCeilLinear(a,target));}

reference.title: binary-search introduction
reference.approach: the separate floor and ceiling searches
reference.adaptation: The current sheet has no public article link for this combined question. These searches follow the public introductory lesson; they return values rather than indices to match the combined practice problem. The Java here implements those published steps.

84.problem: Find the first and last indices of a target in a sorted array.
84.assumptions: Return [-1,-1] if absent. Returned endpoints are inclusive.

example.explanation: Finding the 4 at index 2 is not enough. Search left to reach index 1, and separately search right to reach index 3.

84.baseline: Scan once and record the first and latest matches in O(n) time.
84.approach:
A normal binary search stops at any match. Here, remember the match and keep looking. To find the first occurrence, continue to its left. To find the last, continue to its right.

If you never find a match, the saved answer stays -1. The same rule handles an empty array.
steps: Run a binary search that saves matches and continues left.
Run another search that saves matches and continues right.
Return the two saved indices.
pitfalls: Do not linearly expand from a found match; a long block of duplicates would cost O(n).
Handle absence before interpreting the boundaries as matching indices.
tests: Random r=new Random(84);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(7);Arrays.sort(a);int target=r.nextInt(9)-1;assert Arrays.equals(range(a,target),rangeLinear(a,target));}

reference.title: last-occurrence
reference.approach: saving a matching index and continuing the binary search
reference.adaptation: The current sheet links a last-occurrence lesson here. To cover both parts of this tracker question, the first-occurrence method mirrors it by continuing left after a match.

85.problem: Count how many times a target appears in a sorted array.
85.assumptions: Return zero when absent. Duplicates are adjacent because the input is sorted.

example.explanation: The equal-value block starts at lower bound 1 and ends just before upper bound 4. Its length is 4−1=3.

85.baseline: Count matches in a full O(n) scan.
85.approach:
Equal values sit together in a sorted array. Find the start of that block and the position just after it. Their difference is the number of matching values.

For the example, the block occupies indices 1, 2 and 3. The position after it is 4, so the count is 4 - 1 = 3.
steps: Find the first value at least as large as the target using lower bound.
Return zero if that position is outside the array or contains another value.
Find the first value strictly larger using upper bound. Subtract the starting position.
pitfalls: Use the difference of half-open boundaries, without adding one.
The two comparisons must differ on equality.
tests: Random r=new Random(85);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(20)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(7);Arrays.sort(a);int target=r.nextInt(9)-1;assert occurrences(a,target)==countLinear(a,target);}

reference.title: count-occurrences
reference.approach: a linear count, then lower and upper bounds

86.problem: Find a target in a rotated ascending array of distinct values.
86.assumptions: Return its index or -1. There is at most one rotation point.

example.explanation: The first midpoint holds 12. The left part [8, 10, 12] is sorted, but 4 cannot be inside it. Keep the right part and find 4 at index 4.

86.baseline: Scan all values in O(n) time.
86.approach:
A rotation creates one break in the sorted order. Splitting at the middle leaves at least one half without that break.

Find that sorted half and compare the target with its endpoints. If the target fits between them, search there. Otherwise, search the other half. Check the midpoint itself before discarding either side.
steps: Check midpoint equality first.
Identify the sorted half using its endpoint values.
Keep the half whose range can contain the target, excluding the failed midpoint.
pitfalls: Duplicates can make sorted-half detection ambiguous; use the separate duplicate-aware variant.
Include the outer endpoint and exclude the already-tested midpoint in range checks.
tests: for(int n=1;n<20;n++)for(int shift=0;shift<n;shift++){int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=(i+shift)%n;for(int x=0;x<n;x++)assert a[rotatedSearch(a,x)]==x;}
for(int n=1;n<20;n++)for(int shift=0;shift<n;shift++){int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=((i+shift)%n)*2;for(int x=-1;x<=2*n;x++)assert rotatedSearch(a,x)==rotatedLinear(a,x);}

rows: 4 is outside the sorted left range [8, 12]. Set low to 3.

reference.title: rotated-array search
reference.approach: a linear scan, then searching the identifiable sorted half

87.problem: Determine whether a target exists in a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicates.
87.assumptions: Return a boolean. Worst-case logarithmic time cannot be guaranteed with arbitrary duplicates.

example.explanation: The first, middle and last values are all 1. They tell us nothing about which half holds 0. Remove the equal ends, then search the smaller range.

87.baseline: A linear scan is O(n) and remains a useful worst-case baseline.
87.approach:
Start with the same sorted-half search. Duplicates add one awkward case: the left, middle and right values can all be equal even though a different value is hidden inside.

Check the midpoint against the target first. If it misses, the equal endpoints miss too, so remove those two positions and try again. You may only remove a few positions per step, which explains the linear worst case.
steps: Check midpoint equality.
If all three boundary values are equal, move both outer boundaries inward.
Otherwise use the identifiable sorted half to choose the next interval.
87.time: O(n) worst case; often O(log n) when duplicate ambiguity is limited.
pitfalls: Claiming unconditional O(log n) ignores arrays dominated by the same value.
Test midpoint equality before discarding equal endpoints.
tests: Random r=new Random(87);for(int t=0;t<300;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(15);int[] sorted=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)sorted[i]=r.nextInt(5);Arrays.sort(sorted);for(int shift=0;shift<n;shift++){int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=sorted[(i+shift)%n];for(int target=-1;target<=5;target++)assert rotatedContains(a,target)==containsLinear(a,target);}}

reference.title: rotated-array search with duplicates
reference.approach: shrinking equal endpoints before using the sorted-half test

88.problem: Find the minimum value in a rotated ascending array of distinct values.
88.assumptions: The array is nonempty. An unrotated array is valid.

example.explanation: The left block [8, 10, 12] is sorted. Remember its smallest value, 8, and look in the other block. There you find 2, which improves the answer.

88.baseline: Scan for the smallest value in O(n) time.
88.approach:
Find a half that is sorted. Its first value is its smallest, so save that value before skipping the whole half. Nothing else in that half can improve it.

Repeat on what remains. The saved answer remembers the best value even after its position has left the search range.
steps: Start the saved answer at the first array value.
If the left half is sorted, save its first value and search right.
Otherwise save the midpoint value, the start of the sorted right half, and search left.
pitfalls: Save the sorted half’s minimum before skipping that half.
This version assumes distinct values. Duplicates can hide which half contains the break.
tests: for(int n=1;n<30;n++)for(int shift=0;shift<n;shift++){int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=((i+shift)%n)*3-20;assert minimum(a)==minimumLinear(a);}

reference.title: rotated-minimum
reference.approach: saving the minimum of each sorted half before discarding it
reference.adaptation: The source prose mixes two variants. This explanation follows its Java saved-minimum method, using int[] and an overflow-safe midpoint.

89.problem: Determine the rotation offset of a sorted array with distinct values.
89.assumptions: Return the index of the minimum, interpreted as the number of right rotations modulo n. Return zero for empty input.

example.explanation: The minimum 1 is at index 2. Right-rotating [1,2,3,4,5] twice produces the input.

89.baseline: Scan for the smallest element’s index in O(n) time.
89.approach:
The smallest number began at index 0. Every right rotation moves it one place to the right, wrapping around at the end. Its current index therefore gives the rotation count modulo the length.

Use the saved-minimum search, but save the minimum’s index too. If the remaining range is already sorted, its first value is the only candidate you still need to check.
steps: Start with the first element as the smallest value seen, at index 0.
Record a sorted half’s first value and index if it is smaller. Then discard that half.
Return the index saved for the smallest value.
pitfalls: Left rotation count differs: for nonempty input it is (n−answer)%n.
The historical number of rotations is not recoverable; only its value modulo n is.
tests: for(int n=1;n<30;n++)for(int shift=0;shift<n;shift++){int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=((i+shift)%n)*3-20;assert rotations(a)==rotationsLinear(a);assert rotations(a)==(n-shift)%n;}

reference.title: rotation-count
reference.approach: saving the minimum value and its index
reference.adaptation: The candidate starts at the first element, so a single Integer.MAX_VALUE still returns index 0. Empty input returns 0 as an added convenience.

90.problem: Find the single value in a sorted array where every other value appears exactly twice.
90.assumptions: The array has odd positive length and satisfies the multiplicity promise.

example.explanation: Pairs before 7 begin at even indices: 0 and 2. After 7, the pair of 9s begins at odd index 5. The single number shifts the pairing by one place.

90.baseline: Check pairs from the start: indices 0 and 1, then 2 and 3, and so on. Return the first value whose partner differs, or the last value if every earlier pair matches.
90.approach:
Before the single number, pairs occupy (0, 1), (2, 3), and so on. After it, their starting indices become odd.

Move the midpoint to an even index. If it matches the next value, that pair is still before the single number, so skip it. If it does not match, the single number is there or farther left.
steps: Search between indices zero and n−1.
Round mid down to even.
Skip a matching pair with lo=mid+2; otherwise set hi=mid.
pitfalls: The proof depends on sorted adjacent pairs, not merely an odd array length.
Aligning mid first keeps mid+1 valid while lo<hi.
tests: for(int groups=1;groups<25;groups++)for(int single=0;single<groups;single++){int[] a=new int[2*groups-1];int at=0;for(int value=0;value<groups;value++){a[at++]=value;if(value!=single)a[at++]=value;}assert singleSorted(a)==single;assert singleSorted(a)==singleLinear(a);}

reference.title: single-element search
reference.approach: checking pairs, then binary search on even-index pairs

91.problem: Return an index of an element strictly larger than its adjacent neighbors.
91.assumptions: Adjacent values are unequal. Missing neighbors outside the array are treated as negative infinity; return -1 for empty input.

example.explanation: The slope from 2 to 3 rises, so a peak exists on that side. The value 3 then exceeds both neighbors.

91.baseline: Scan every index and check its neighbors in O(n) time.
91.approach:
Look at the step from mid to mid + 1. If it rises, follow it right. The values will either eventually fall, creating a peak, or reach the end with the last value as a peak.

If the step falls, use the same reasoning toward the left. Keep mid in that case: it could already be the peak.
steps: Compare a[mid] with a[mid+1].
On a rise, move lo to mid+1; otherwise move hi to mid.
Return the remaining index; it need not be the global maximum.
pitfalls: This finds any peak, not necessarily the greatest value.
Equal adjacent values require a different definition or additional handling for strict peaks.
tests: Random r=new Random(91);for(int t=0;t<300;t++){int n=1+r.nextInt(30);int[] a=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){do{a[i]=r.nextInt(40);}while(i>0&&a[i]==a[i-1]);}int at=peak(a);assert at>=0&&at<n;assert at==0||a[at]>a[at-1];assert at==n-1||a[at]>a[at+1];assert peakLinear(a)>=0;}

reference.title: peak-element
reference.approach: a neighbour scan, then binary search following a rising side

example.explanation: 5²=25 is at most 28, while 6²=36 exceeds it. The answer is the last integer whose square fits.

92.baseline: Try successive integers until the next square exceeds n, taking O(sqrt(n)) time.
92.approach: Binary search the monotone predicate x²<=n. Test it as x<=n/x for positive x, avoiding overflow in the square.
steps: Handle zero separately.
Search positive candidates up to min(n,3037000499).
Keep the greatest candidate satisfying the division comparison.
pitfalls: mid*mid can overflow long before the comparison.
A floating-point square root needs careful integer correction near large perfect squares.

93.problem: Find an integer x such that xⁿ equals m, or report that no exact nonnegative root exists.
93.assumptions: n>0 and m>=0. Return -1 when the root is not an integer.

example.explanation: The cubes below 3 are too small, 3³ equals 27, and larger positive candidates have larger cubes.

93.baseline: Try roots in increasing order, repeatedly multiplying to compare with m.
93.approach: For nonnegative roots, xⁿ is monotone. Binary search x and stop multiplication as soon as the next product would exceed m. Division detects that condition without overflowing long.
steps: Handle m=0 and n=1 directly.
Compare each candidate power to m using bounded multiplication.
Move left or right based on the comparison; return only on exact equality.
93.time: O(n log m) upper bound; comparisons stop early once the target is exceeded.
pitfalls: Math.pow uses floating-point arithmetic and cannot safely test exact large integer equality.
Odd roots of negative values are a separate variant; this contract covers m>=0.

94.problem: Find the smallest integer eating speed that finishes all banana piles within h hours.
94.assumptions: Each positive pile consumes its own whole-number hours; an hour cannot be shared between piles. Return -1 if h is too small.

example.explanation: At speed 4, the piles need 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 hours. At speed 3, they need 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 hours, which is too long.

94.baseline: Try every speed from 1 to the largest pile, costing O(n×maxPile).
94.approach:
Try a speed and count the hours it needs. A pile of 9 at speed 4 needs three hours, even though its last hour eats only one banana. Round each pile separately.

If a speed finishes on time, faster speeds work too. If it is too slow, every smaller speed fails too. Use those two facts to discard half the speeds at each step.
steps: Reject h smaller than the number of nonempty piles.
Binary search speeds between one and the maximum pile.
Use long ceiling division and stop counting once the hour budget is exceeded.
pitfalls: Use ceiling division per pile, not once after summing all bananas.
Integer arithmetic in pile+speed−1 needs promotion to long.
tests: Random r=new Random(94);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(8)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(20);int h=1+r.nextInt(40);assert minSpeed(a,h)==minSpeedLinear(a,h);}

reference.title: Koko eating bananas
reference.approach: trying speeds, then binary searching with an hours-check helper
reference.adaptation: The ceiling-division addition uses long before division to avoid int overflow. Empty input and impossible hour budgets are handled explicitly.

95.problem: Find the earliest day on which m bouquets of k adjacent bloomed flowers can be made.
95.assumptions: Each flower is used at most once. Bloom days are positive. Return -1 if there are too few flowers; m=0 needs day zero.

example.explanation: On day 2, three flowers have bloomed, but none are neighbours. On day 5, all five have bloomed, so use positions 0–1 and 2–3 for two bouquets.

95.baseline: Check each day until a feasible arrangement appears, repeating the scan over a potentially large date range.
95.approach:
For one trial day, walk along the garden. Count consecutive flowers that have bloomed. Each time the count reaches k, make a bouquet and reset it; those flowers are now used. An unbloomed flower also resets the count because it breaks the row.

Once a day works, every later day works. Search earlier after success and later after failure.
steps: Check m×k against the array length using long.
Binary search between the earliest and latest bloom dates.
For each day, greedily count nonoverlapping blocks of k consecutive bloomed flowers.
pitfalls: Counting all bloomed flowers ignores adjacency.
Reset the run after forming a bouquet to prevent reusing flowers.
tests: Random r=new Random(95);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(9)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(10);int m=r.nextInt(5),k=1+r.nextInt(4);assert bouquetDay(a,m,k)==bouquetLinear(a,m,k);}

reference.title: minimum bouquet day
reference.approach: counting adjacent groups and binary searching days with a saved answer

96.problem: Find the smallest positive divisor for which the sum of rounded-up quotients is at most a threshold.
96.assumptions: All array values are positive. Return -1 when threshold<n, and zero for empty input.

example.explanation: Divisor 3 gives 1 + 3 + 4 = 8, which is too much. Divisor 4 gives 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, which fits.

96.baseline: Try every divisor up to the largest value in O(n×maxValue) time.
96.approach:
A larger divisor makes each rounded-up result smaller or leaves it unchanged. So once a divisor works, every larger one works too.

Try the middle divisor. If its sum fits the threshold, keep it as an option and look for a smaller divisor. If the sum is too large, all smaller divisors can be skipped.
steps: The possible divisors start at 1 and need not exceed the largest array value.
For a trial divisor, round up each division separately and add the results.
If the total fits, search smaller divisors; otherwise search larger ones.
pitfalls: Each positive value contributes at least one, establishing the impossibility condition.
Integer division without rounding up underestimates the required sum.
tests: Random r=new Random(96);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(8)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(20);int threshold=1+r.nextInt(40);assert smallestDivisor(a,threshold)==divisorLinear(a,threshold);}

reference.title: smallest-divisor
reference.approach: a trial-divisor check and binary search, with the two direct-answer cases
reference.adaptation: The addition before division and the running sum use long to avoid int overflow. Impossible thresholds and empty input are handled explicitly.

97.problem: Find the smallest ship capacity that delivers packages in their given order within D days.
97.assumptions: Package weights are positive, cannot be split, and must stay in order. D>0; unused days are allowed.

example.explanation: With capacity 6, ship [2, 3], then [4, 2], then [5]. Capacity 5 needs four days: [2, 3], [4], [2], [5].

97.baseline: Try capacities from the heaviest package to the total weight, scanning each candidate.
97.approach:
For a trial capacity, load as many packages as fit, keeping their order. Start a new day only when the next package would overflow. Leaving space earlier cannot help: it only leaves more packages for later.

A larger capacity cannot need more days. If the trial fits the deadline, try a smaller capacity; otherwise try a larger one.
steps: Set the lower bound to the largest weight and upper bound to the total.
Count greedy days for each candidate capacity.
Search for the first capacity needing at most D days.
pitfalls: Sorting the weights changes the problem because order is fixed.
Capacity must fit the largest single package, regardless of the day count.
tests: Random r=new Random(97);for(int t=0;t<200;t++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(8)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(10);int days=1+r.nextInt(10);assert shipCapacity(a,days)==shipLinear(a,days);}

reference.title: shipping-capacity
reference.approach: loading in order, then binary searching capacity with a saved answer
reference.adaptation: Capacity, load and total weight use long so their sums do not overflow int.

98.problem: Find the kth missing positive integer relative to a strictly increasing positive array.
98.assumptions: k>0. Return long to cover results beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE.

example.explanation: The missing positives are 1,5,6,8,9,… . Before value 7 at index 3, exactly 7−(3+1)=3 positives are missing.

98.baseline: Walk through positive integers, advancing through array entries and counting absent values.
98.approach: At index i, a[i]−(i+1) counts missing positives before a[i]. This count is nondecreasing. Find the first index with at least k missing values; if that index is p, the answer is p+k because exactly p supplied values precede it.
steps: Binary search the missing-count predicate.
Move left when a[mid]−mid−1 >=k.
Return the insertion boundary plus k.
pitfalls: This formula requires distinct, positive, sorted entries.
The result may lie beyond the final array value; boundary n handles that naturally.

99.problem: Place cows in stalls to maximize the minimum distance between any two placed cows.
99.assumptions: Stall coordinates are integers; each stall holds one cow. The array is sorted in place. Return -1 if there are too few stalls and zero for one cow.

example.explanation: Choose stalls 2, 9 and 15. The gaps are 7 and 6, so the minimum is 6. Requiring a gap of 7 allows 2 and 9, but no third stall.

99.baseline: Try each possible distance and test placement, which depends on the potentially large coordinate range.
99.approach:
For a trial gap, place each cow in the earliest stall that is far enough from the previous cow. Waiting for a later stall cannot leave more room for the cows still to come.

If all cows fit, try a bigger gap. If they do not, the gap is too demanding, so try a smaller one. Here success moves the search right because we want the largest working gap.
steps: Sort the coordinates.
Greedily test whether the requested number of cows fits a candidate separation.
Increase the distance after success and decrease it after failure.
99.space: O(log n) sorting stack, O(1) search state.
pitfalls: This maximizes a minimum, so success moves the lower boundary upward.
Coordinate subtraction can overflow int even when each coordinate fits int.
tests: Random r=new Random(99);for(int t=0;t<150;t++){int n=2+r.nextInt(7),cows=2+r.nextInt(n-1);int[] a=new int[n];int position=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){position+=1+r.nextInt(4);a[i]=position;}long best=0;for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<n);mask++){if(Integer.bitCount(mask)!=cows)continue;int last=-1;long gap=Long.MAX_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if((mask&(1<<i))!=0){if(last>=0)gap=Math.min(gap,(long)a[i]-a[last]);last=i;}best=Math.max(best,gap);}assert aggressiveCows(a.clone(),cows)==best;assert cowsLinear(a.clone(),cows)==best;}

reference.title: aggressive-cows
reference.approach: greedy placement and binary search for the largest working distance
reference.adaptation: Coordinate differences use long. The helper also handles one cow and reports too few stalls explicitly.

100.problem: Assign books in order to exactly m students, minimizing the maximum pages assigned to one student.
100.assumptions: Page counts are positive. Every student receives a nonempty contiguous block, and every book is assigned once. Return -1 when m is invalid.

example.explanation: Give [20, 30] to the first student and [10, 40] to the second. Both read 50 pages. A limit of 49 forces three students.

100.baseline: Try page limits one by one, starting with the largest book. For each limit, assign consecutive books until the next book would exceed it.
100.approach:
A trial limit says how many pages one student may receive. Fill a student’s block before starting the next one. If that needs too many students, increase the limit; otherwise try lowering it.

The check may use fewer than the requested students. That is fine: split a block between two books until everyone has one. Splitting cannot increase a student’s pages, provided there are at least as many books as students.
steps: Search limits from the largest book to total pages.
Count the minimum required groups greedily.
Keep a limit when the group count is at most m.
pitfalls: Do not sort books: the original order is part of the constraint.
At-most-m feasibility implies exactly m only because blocks can be split and m<=n.
tests: Random r=new Random(100);for(int t=0;t<150;t++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(8)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=1+r.nextInt(12);int groups=1+r.nextInt(a.length);long best=Long.MAX_VALUE;for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<(a.length-1));mask++){if(Integer.bitCount(mask)!=groups-1)continue;long sum=0,max=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){sum+=a[i];if(i==a.length-1||(mask&(1<<i))!=0){max=Math.max(max,sum);sum=0;}}best=Math.min(best,max);}assert allocateBooks(a,groups)==best;assert booksLinear(a,groups)==best;}

reference.title: book-allocation
reference.approach: a page-limit check and binary search on the limit
reference.adaptation: The result stays long instead of narrowing back to int, so large page totals remain correct.

101.problem: Split an array into exactly k nonempty contiguous parts, minimizing the largest part sum.
101.assumptions: Values are nonnegative; k must lie between 1 and n. Return -1 for invalid k.

example.explanation: Split as [4, 1, 7] and [3, 2], with sums 12 and 5. At limit 11, the greedy check needs [4, 1], [7, 3], [2]: three parts, so 11 fails.

101.baseline: Try every allowed maximum sum from the largest element to the total. Return the first one that permits at most k parts.
101.approach:
For a trial maximum sum, keep adding numbers to a part until the next would exceed the limit. Then begin another part. If even this packing needs more than k parts, the limit is too small.

If fewer than k parts are needed, split some of them further. Because values are nonnegative, splitting cannot increase a part’s sum. That is why the check can use “at most k” even though the answer requires exactly k.
steps: Bound the answer by max(array) and sum(array).
Greedily count groups under each candidate limit.
Find the first candidate requiring at most k groups.
101.time: O(n log(totalSum−maxValue+1)); the all-zero case finishes immediately.
pitfalls: Negative values break the greedy feasibility proof and the search bounds.
The target is the maximum group sum, not the sum of those maxima over candidate splits.
tests: Random r=new Random(101);for(int t=0;t<150;t++){int[] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(8)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(12);int groups=1+r.nextInt(a.length);long best=Long.MAX_VALUE;for(int mask=0;mask<(1<<(a.length-1));mask++){if(Integer.bitCount(mask)!=groups-1)continue;long sum=0,max=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){sum+=a[i];if(i==a.length-1||(mask&(1<<i))!=0){max=Math.max(max,sum);sum=0;}}best=Math.min(best,max);}assert splitArray(a,groups)==best;assert splitLinear(a,groups)==best;}

reference.title: split-array
reference.approach: a contiguous-group check and binary search with a saved answer
reference.adaptation: Sums and the returned result use long to avoid int overflow.

102.problem: Assign consecutive boards to painters to minimize the completion time when all painters work at the same rate.
102.assumptions: Board lengths are nonnegative and cannot be split. Each painter handles at most one contiguous block; painters may be idle. One length unit takes one time unit.

example.explanation: Assign [10,20,30] to one painter and [40] to the other. The slower block finishes at time 60.

102.baseline: Try every set of contiguous partition boundaries, or use O(p n²) prefix dynamic programming.
102.approach: A proposed finishing time is a capacity limit for each painter. Greedily assign the longest possible prefix to each painter. More available time never increases the required painter count, enabling binary search.
steps: Search from the largest board to the total length.
Count painters needed by a greedy scan.
Accept a time if it uses no more than the available painters.
pitfalls: Extra painters may remain idle; painters>boards is not an impossibility.
If a platform supplies a per-unit rate or output modulus, apply those to the resulting workload according to that platform’s contract.

103.problem: Insert at most k gas stations to minimize the largest distance between adjacent stations.
103.assumptions: Existing positions are sorted and distinct. New positions may be fractional. The result is approximate; return zero for fewer than two stations.

example.explanation: Placing stations at 2.5,5,7.5 divides the original gap into four equal parts.

103.baseline: Keep a count of new stations assigned to each original gap. Add each next station to the gap whose current pieces are longest. Scan all gaps to choose it, and redistribute that gap’s stations evenly.
103.approach:
Instead of placing stations one at a time, ask whether a proposed largest gap is possible. A length-10 gap limited to 2 needs five pieces, so four stations. In general, the count is ceil(gap / limit) - 1.

Add those counts across the original gaps. If they exceed k, allow a larger distance. Otherwise try a smaller one. We search decimal distances because new stations need not sit at integer positions.
steps: Start between zero and the largest original gap.
Check the midpoint by counting the new stations it needs.
Keep the feasible upper end. After 100 halvings, return it as a floating-point approximation.
103.time: O(100n); equivalently O(n log(initialRange/desiredPrecision)) for tolerance-based search.
pitfalls: Do not permanently split only the current longest piece in half. The scan and heap versions redistribute each original gap into equal pieces.
When a gap divides exactly, the number of new stations is one less than the number of pieces.
Compare decimal results with a tolerance, not exact equality.
tests: Random r=new Random(103);for(int t=0;t<150;t++){int[] a=new int[2+r.nextInt(5)];for(int i=1;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=a[i-1]+1+r.nextInt(10);int k=r.nextInt(12);double expected=gasGapScan(a,k);assert Math.abs(minGasGap(a,k)-expected)<1e-6;assert Math.abs(gasGapHeap(a,k)-expected)<1e-9;}

better.explanation: A max heap keeps the longest current piece at the top. Remove that gap, increase its station count, and put back its new piece length. This avoids scanning every gap for each station.

reference.title: gas-station spacing
reference.approach: scanning gaps, using a max heap, then binary search on distance
reference.adaptation: The station count uses ceil(gap / limit) - 1 to handle exact division correctly. Differences are widened before subtraction, and the search uses 100 bounded halvings instead of a tolerance-based loop.

104.problem: Find the middle value of the sorted order formed by two sorted arrays. If there are two middle values, return their average.
104.assumptions: Both arrays are sorted in increasing or equal order. One may be empty, but they cannot both be empty. Values may repeat.

example.explanation: The combined order is [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8]. Its middle values are 3 and 5, so the median is (3 + 5) / 2 = 4.

104.baseline: Copy both arrays into one array and sort it. Then read the middle value or average the two middle values. This is easy to check, but it sorts values that were already in order.
104.approach:
Imagine a line through the combined sorted order, with half the values on each side. For an odd total, put the extra value on the left. We do not need to build that combined array. We only need to decide how many values each input contributes to the left side.

Suppose we take cutA values from a. Then we must take leftSize − cutA values from b. Because each input is already sorted, we only compare the four values next to the cuts. The last selected value from a must not exceed the first unselected value from b, and the same must hold in the other direction.

If a has a selected value that is too large, take fewer values from a. Otherwise, take more. This lets us binary search the cut in the shorter array. Once the cuts fit, the median is the largest value on the left, or its average with the smallest value on the right.
steps: Set leftSize to (n + m + 1) / 2. Search how many values to take from the shorter array, from 0 through its full length.
For each cut in a, calculate the cut in b. Read the four neighbouring values; treat a missing left value as minus infinity and a missing right value as plus infinity.
If leftA > rightB, move the cut in a left. If leftB > rightA, move it right.
When both comparisons pass, use the two values around the combined middle to return the median.
104.space: O(1); the optional swap recursion has depth at most one.
pitfalls: Average the two central values using a wide type before converting to double.
The cross-boundary comparisons are what validate the combined ordering.
tests: Random r=new Random(104);for(int run=0;run<300;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(16)],b=new int[1+r.nextInt(16)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;for(int i=0;i<b.length;i++)b[i]=r.nextInt(31)-15;Arrays.sort(a);Arrays.sort(b);double expected=medianBySorting(a,b);assert medianByWalking(a,b)==expected;assert median(a,b)==expected;}
boolean rejected=false;try{median(new int[]{},new int[]{});}catch(IllegalArgumentException e){rejected=true;}assert rejected;
104.baselineTime: O((n + m) log(n + m)) time and O(n + m) extra space.

better.explanation: Walk through the arrays as if you were merging them: take the smaller next value each time. Stop when you reach the middle. Keep only the last two values you took; an even-length answer needs both of them.

reference.title: Median of 2 Sorted Arrays
reference.approach: Combine and sort, merge only to the middle, then binary search the partition in the shorter array.
reference.adaptation: The three approaches and Java control flow were checked against the public lesson. These standalone methods use long boundary values and reject two empty inputs.

105.problem: Find the value at position k when two sorted arrays are combined in sorted order. Position 1 means the smallest value.
105.assumptions: The inputs are sorted in increasing or equal order. Repeated values occupy separate positions. Return −1 for a k outside 1 through n + m.

example.explanation: The combined order starts 1, 2, 4, 6. The fourth value is 6.

105.baseline: Copy all the values into one list, sort it, and read index k − 1. Subtract one because Java indexes start at zero.
105.approach:
Put exactly k values on the left of an imaginary dividing line. If every value on the left is at most every value on the right, the largest value on the left must be the kth value.

Take cutA values from a and k − cutA from b. Only the values next to the two cuts can break the sorted order: the rest of each input is already sorted. Check leftA ≤ rightB and leftB ≤ rightA. If the first comparison fails, take fewer from a. If the second fails, take more from a.

The starting bounds matter. We cannot take more than k values or more than a contains. We also must take at least k − b.length from a if b is too short to supply all k values. Binary search within those bounds in the shorter array.
steps: Search the shorter input. Set low = max(0, k − m) and high = min(k, n).
Choose cutA halfway between low and high. The other cut is k − cutA.
Compare the last selected and first unselected values across the two arrays. Move cutA left or right when a comparison fails.
When both comparisons pass, return max(leftA, leftB).
pitfalls: k counts values, so the left side must contain k values, not k − 1.
Bounds based on k keep the second cut inside b. Searching 0 through n without those bounds can access an invalid index.
An absent left or right neighbour uses a sentinel. It does not add an actual value to the combined order.
tests: Random r=new Random(105);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(12)],b=new int[1+r.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(11);for(int i=0;i<b.length;i++)b[i]=r.nextInt(11);Arrays.sort(a);Arrays.sort(b);int[] all=new int[a.length+b.length];System.arraycopy(a,0,all,0,a.length);System.arraycopy(b,0,all,a.length,b.length);Arrays.sort(all);for(int k=1;k<=all.length;k++)assert kth(a,b,k)==all[k-1];}
assert kth(new int[]{},new int[]{},1)==-1;assert kth(new int[]{1},new int[]{2},0)==-1;assert kth(new int[]{1},new int[]{2},3)==-1;

Random r=new Random(1051);for(int run=0;run<200;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(12)],b=new int[1+r.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(21)-10;for(int i=0;i<b.length;i++)b[i]=r.nextInt(21)-10;Arrays.sort(a);Arrays.sort(b);for(int k=1;k<=a.length+b.length;k++){int expected=kthBySorting(a,b,k);assert kthByWalking(a,b,k)==expected;assert kth(a,b,k)==expected;}}
105.baselineTime: O((n + m) log(n + m)) time and O(n + m) extra space.

better.explanation: Compare the next unused values in the two arrays and take the smaller one. After taking k values, the last one taken is the answer. If one array runs out, keep taking values from the other.

reference.title: Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays
reference.approach: Combine and sort, walk through k merged values, then binary search a valid partition.
reference.adaptation: The three Java approaches were checked. The merge walk uses one loop with an exhausted-array check. The partition uses long sentinels; invalid k returns −1 as in the lesson.

106.problem: Return the index of the row with the most ones. If rows tie, return the earliest row. If the matrix has no ones, return −1.
106.assumptions: The matrix is rectangular and contains only 0 and 1. Each row has all its zeros before its ones. Columns do not need to be sorted. An empty matrix returns −1.

example.explanation: Rows 1 and 2 each contain three ones. Row 1 wins because it comes first.

106.baseline: Count the ones in each row. Replace the best row only when you find a strictly larger count, so equal counts keep the earlier row.
106.approach:
Start at the top-right cell. A 1 lets us move one step left and record this row as the best so far. A 0 tells us that everything farther left in this row is also 0, so we move down.

Do not move back to the right when you change rows. The current column is the next position a row must fill with a 1 to beat our record. A row with an equal number of ones has a 0 at that position, so it cannot replace the earlier row.

The pointer moves left at most columns times and down at most rows times. That is why this walk avoids scanning the whole matrix.
steps: Start at row 0 and the last column, with answer −1.
On a 1, save the row and move left. This row has beaten the previous count.
On a 0, move down without changing the column.
Return the last saved row when the pointer leaves the matrix.
106.time: O(rows+columns), because the column pointer only moves left.
pitfalls: Resetting the column for every row loses the linear bound.
The answer convention for an all-zero matrix varies; this version returns -1.
tests: Random r=new Random(106);for(int run=0;run<500;run++){int[][] a=new int[1+r.nextInt(12)][1+r.nextInt(12)];for(int[] row:a){int start=r.nextInt(row.length+1);Arrays.fill(row,start,row.length,1);}int expected=rowMostOnesByCounting(a);assert rowMostOnesByBinarySearch(a)==expected;assert rowMostOnes(a)==expected;}
106.baselineTime: O(rows × columns) time and O(1) extra space.

better.explanation: In a sorted row, finding the first 1 is enough. If it is at column c, the row contains columns − c ones. Use binary search to find that first 1 in every row.

rows: Left; row 0 has at least 2 ones.
Move down twice. The tie in row 2 does not replace row 1.

reference.title: Find the Row with Maximum 1s in a Sorted Binary Matrix
reference.approach: Count every row, binary search each first 1, then walk left/down from the top-right.
reference.adaptation: All three Java approaches were checked. The methods also return −1 for empty input.

107.problem: Return whether a target value appears in a matrix that is sorted when read row by row.
107.assumptions: All rows have the same length. Each row is sorted, and every row starts with a value greater than the last value of the previous row. Empty input returns false.

example.explanation: Reading row by row gives [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 18]. Position 4 in that order is row 1, column 1, which holds 14.

107.baseline: Visit every cell and compare it with the target. Return true on a match and false after checking them all.
107.approach:
Picture the rows placed end to end. The extra rule about where each row starts makes that whole sequence sorted. We can therefore use ordinary binary search without actually copying the values into a new array.

For a position mid in this imaginary array, mid / columns tells us the row and mid % columns tells us the column. With 3 columns, position 4 becomes row 1, column 1. Read that cell, compare it with the target, and discard half of the remaining positions.
steps: Search positions 0 through rows × columns − 1.
Convert the middle position to a row and column using division and remainder.
Return true on equality. If the cell is smaller, move low past it; otherwise move high before it.
If no positions remain, return false.
pitfalls: Row and column sortedness alone is insufficient; the inter-row ordering condition is stronger.
Use long for the virtual size and midpoint.
tests: Random r=new Random(107);for(int run=0;run<200;run++){int rows=1+r.nextInt(8),cols=1+r.nextInt(8);int[][] a=new int[rows][cols];int value=-100;for(int[] row:a)for(int c=0;c<cols;c++){value+=1+r.nextInt(4);row[c]=value;}for(int target=-105;target<=value+5;target++)assert searchMatrix(a,target)==searchByScanning(a,target);}
107.baselineTime: O(rows × columns) time and O(1) extra space.

reference.title: Search in a Sorted 2D Matrix Using Binary Search
reference.approach: Full scan, then binary search using virtual row-by-row indices.
reference.adaptation: The public Java implementations were checked. The virtual positions use long so multiplying the dimensions cannot overflow an int.

108.problem: Search a matrix sorted independently along every row and every column.
108.assumptions: The matrix is rectangular. Values may repeat; the last value of one row may exceed the first of the next.

example.explanation: Start at 7 in the top-right. Move left to 4 because 7 is too large, then down to 5 and 6 because those cells are too small.

108.baseline: Visit every cell and look for a match. This works even without sorted rows or columns.
108.approach:
Stand at the top-right corner of the remaining rectangle. The values to your left are no larger, and the values below you are no smaller. This gives each comparison a clear direction.

If the current value is too large, every value below it in that column is also too large. Remove that column by moving left. If the current value is too small, every value to its left in that row is also too small. Remove that row by moving down.

Each move removes a row or a column. The search ends when it finds the target or runs out of cells. Reading the entire matrix row by row would not necessarily give a sorted array, so the previous question’s flattening trick does not apply here.
steps: Start at row zero and the last column.
Move left when the current value exceeds target.
Move down when it is below target; stop on equality or when leaving the matrix.
pitfalls: A flattened binary search is invalid unless the stronger global row-major ordering also holds.
Starting at the top-left gives no safe elimination direction when its value is too small.
tests: Random r=new Random(108);for(int run=0;run<300;run++){int rows=1+r.nextInt(8),cols=1+r.nextInt(8);int[][] a=new int[rows][cols];for(int i=0;i<rows;i++)for(int j=0;j<cols;j++){int prev=-20;if(i>0)prev=Math.max(prev,a[i-1][j]);if(j>0)prev=Math.max(prev,a[i][j-1]);a[i][j]=prev+r.nextInt(4);}for(int target=-22;target<=a[rows-1][cols-1]+2;target++)assert staircaseSearch(a,target)==searchByScanning(a,target);}
108.baselineTime: O(rows × columns) time and O(1) extra space.

reference.title: Search in a Row and Column-Wise Sorted Matrix
reference.approach: Full scan, then staircase search starting at the top-right.
reference.adaptation: The public lesson and optimal Java solution were checked. The implementation follows the same row/column elimination.

109.problem: Find any cell that is bigger than each of its neighbours above, below, left and right. Return its row and column.
109.assumptions: The matrix is rectangular and neighbouring cells have different values. The source uses a −1 outside border with nonnegative values. Here, missing neighbours are ignored, which also supports negative values. Empty input returns an empty pair.

example.explanation: The cell 4 exceeds its left and lower neighbors; its other two neighbors are outside the matrix. Either listed peak is a valid answer.

109.baseline: Check every cell against its existing neighbours. The first cell that beats all of them is a valid answer. Diagonal cells do not count.
109.approach:
Choose the middle row, then find the largest value in that row. It already beats its immediate left and right neighbours: neither can be larger, and adjacent values cannot be equal. We only need a decision about the vertical direction.

Compare this row maximum with the cell directly below it. If the lower cell is larger, move the search below the middle row. If it is smaller, keep the middle row and the rows above it. In each case there is still a peak on the side we keep.

Repeat until one row remains, then return its largest value. The row maximum takes care of the horizontal neighbours, and the search choices take care of the vertical neighbours. This finds a local peak; it does not promise the largest value in the whole matrix.
steps: Start with all row indices, from 0 through rows − 1.
While low < high, find the largest value in the middle row.
If it is larger than the cell below, set high = mid. Otherwise set low = mid + 1.
Find the largest value in the final row and return its coordinates.
109.time: O(columns × (1 + log rows)); the final row also needs one scan.
pitfalls: The matrix need not be sorted. Only neighbouring values must be unequal.
A peak beats its four direct neighbours, not diagonal cells and not necessarily every cell.
Keep mid when moving high: that row may contain the answer. Using high = mid − 1 can skip it.
tests: Random r=new Random(109);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[][] a=new int[5][7];List<Integer> values=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<35;i++)values.add(i);Collections.shuffle(values,r);for(int i=0;i<35;i++)a[i/7][i%7]=values.get(i);int[] p=peak2D(a);int row=p[0],col=p[1],v=a[row][col];assert row==0||v>a[row-1][col];assert row==4||v>a[row+1][col];assert col==0||v>a[row][col-1];assert col==6||v>a[row][col+1];}

Random r=new Random(1091);for(int run=0;run<1000;run++){int rows=1+r.nextInt(8),cols=1+r.nextInt(8);int[][] a=new int[rows][cols];List<Integer> values=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<rows*cols;i++)values.add(i-40);Collections.shuffle(values,r);for(int i=0;i<rows*cols;i++)a[i/cols][i%cols]=values.get(i);int[] p=peak2D(a),q=peakByScanning(a);assert q.length==2;int row=p[0],col=p[1],v=a[row][col];assert row==0||v>a[row-1][col];assert row+1==rows||v>a[row+1][col];assert col==0||v>a[row][col-1];assert col+1==cols||v>a[row][col+1];}
109.baselineTime: O(rows × columns) time and O(1) extra space.

rows: The cell below is 2. Keep row 0 by setting high = 0.
Return [0, 1]. Its actual neighbours are 1 and 2.

reference.title: Find a Peak Element in a 2D Matrix Using Binary Search
reference.approach: Scan neighbours, then binary search rows using each middle row’s maximum.
reference.adaptation: The public Java solution searches rows, so this guide now uses that variant. Missing neighbours are ignored instead of using −1, allowing the existing negative-value tests.

110.problem: Find the median value in a row-wise sorted matrix.
110.assumptions: The matrix is nonempty and rectangular, with an odd total cell count. Columns need not be sorted.

example.explanation: The nine values in sorted order are 1 through 9. Four values come before 5 and four after it, so 5 is the middle value.

110.baseline: Collect all cells in one list, sort it, and return the value at index size / 2. This is a useful way to check the faster answer.
110.approach:
Instead of searching for a cell position, guess a value. Ask how many cells are less than or equal to that guess. For nine cells, the median is the first value that reaches a count of at least five.

Each row is sorted, so its upper bound tells us how many values are at most the guess. Add those counts across all rows. If the total is at most half the number of cells, the guess is too small. Otherwise the guess is large enough, and we can try smaller values.

The smallest and largest values must be at row ends, so those give the starting bounds. We keep halving the range until one value remains. Duplicates work too: the count can jump past the middle, and the first value that causes that jump is the median.
steps: Find the smallest row-first value and the largest row-last value.
Guess the middle value of that range. Use upper bound in each row to count cells ≤ the guess.
If the count is at most total / 2, set low = mid + 1. Otherwise set high = mid.
Return the single value left when low equals high.
110.time: O(rows + rows × log(columns + 1) × log(valueRange + 1)). The first term finds the bounds. Int values need at most 32 value-search steps.
pitfalls: Count <=mid, not just <mid, to handle duplicates correctly.
Use long boundaries so max−min cannot overflow for the full int range.
An even number of cells needs an explicitly defined lower, upper, or averaged median.
tests: Random r=new Random(110);for(int run=0;run<500;run++){int rows=1+2*r.nextInt(5),cols=1+2*r.nextInt(5);int[][] a=new int[rows][cols];for(int[] row:a){for(int c=0;c<cols;c++)row[c]=r.nextInt(31)-15;Arrays.sort(row);}assert matrixMedian(a)==matrixMedianBySorting(a);}
110.baselineTime: O(N log N) time and O(N) extra space, where N is the number of cells.

reference.title: Median of a Row-Wise Sorted Matrix
reference.approach: Flatten and sort, then search the answer value using an upper bound in each row.
reference.adaptation: The optimal Java solution was checked. Long bounds and counts handle the full int range, and empty or even-sized inputs are rejected explicitly.

111.problem: Remove the first and last parenthesis from every primitive component of a valid parentheses string.
111.assumptions: Input consists only of balanced parentheses. A primitive component cannot be split into two nonempty balanced strings.

example.explanation: The two primitive components are (()()) and (()). Removing each outer pair leaves ()() and ().

111.baseline: Split the input into primitive substrings, trim each, and concatenate, requiring storage for intermediate pieces.
111.approach: Track nesting depth. An opening parenthesis is outermost exactly when depth is zero before it. A closing parenthesis is outermost exactly when depth becomes zero after it.
steps: For an opening parenthesis, append only if the previous depth was positive, then increment depth.
For a closing parenthesis, decrement depth first and append only if the new depth is positive.
Use a StringBuilder to avoid repeated immutable-string copying.
111.space: O(n) for output; O(1) conceptual scan state, plus toCharArray’s O(n) copy.
pitfalls: Incrementing/decrementing at the wrong moment keeps or removes the wrong pair.
This version assumes valid parentheses rather than validating malformed input.

112.problem: Reverse the order of words, removing leading/trailing spaces and collapsing runs of spaces to one.
112.assumptions: The saved link is the word-order problem. The title also mentions palindrome checking, so a separate exact-character palindrome helper is included. Word separators here are ordinary spaces.

example.explanation: Read complete words from right to left. Append each extracted word after a single separator, so its letters remain in their original order.

112.baseline: Split into a list of words, reverse the list, and join. This is straightforward but creates intermediate word objects.
112.approach: Scan backward to find the last nonspace character, then the start of that word. Append that interval and repeat. This directly emits the required order without reversing characters within a word.
steps: Skip spaces from the right.
Locate the preceding word boundary.
Append that word, inserting one space only between output words.
112.space: O(n) output for word reversal; O(1) for palindrome checking.
pitfalls: Reversing every character produces reversed spelling, which is a different operation.
The palindrome helper is case-sensitive and includes punctuation; ignoring them requires a different contract.
charAt compares UTF-16 units, not user-perceived grapheme clusters.
tests: assert reverseWords("  the sky   is blue  ").equals("blue is sky the");

113.problem: Return the largest-valued odd substring of a decimal digit string.
113.assumptions: The input contains decimal digits. Return an empty string if no odd digit exists; do not convert the potentially huge value to an integer.

example.explanation: The rightmost odd digit is 5. Every odd candidate must end at an odd digit, and keeping all earlier digits gives the largest available prefix value.

113.baseline: Enumerate substrings, identify odd ones, and compare their numeric values or lengths, doing unnecessary quadratic work.
113.approach: An integer is odd exactly when its final digit is odd. End at the rightmost odd digit and retain the full prefix: removing earlier nonnegative decimal digits cannot make the value larger. This also handles values far beyond machine integer ranges.
steps: Scan digits from right to left.
Stop at the first odd digit.
Return the prefix through that position, or empty when none exists.
113.space: O(n) for the returned substring in modern Java; O(1) scan state.
pitfalls: The answer is a prefix, not just the largest odd single digit.
Integer.parseInt or Long.parseLong can overflow on valid long inputs.

114.problem: Return the longest prefix shared by every string in an array.
114.assumptions: An empty array or any empty member yields an empty prefix. Strings are compared by UTF-16 code units.

example.explanation: All strings share f and l. At the third position, o differs from i, so the shared prefix stops before that position.

114.baseline: Sort the strings and compare only the first and last; sorting performs work unrelated to the needed prefix.
114.approach: The prefix can only shrink as strings are considered. Compare the current common-prefix length against each next string, reducing it at the first mismatch.
steps: Initialize the possible length to the first string’s length.
For each remaining string, compare only up to the current possible length.
Return the corresponding prefix of the first string.
114.time: O(S), where S is the total number of input characters examined; at most total input size.
114.space: O(p) for the returned prefix, O(1) auxiliary state.
pitfalls: Check the next string’s length before reading its character.
A shared substring somewhere inside every word is not necessarily a prefix.

115.problem: Check whether two strings have the same character-repetition structure under a one-to-one renaming.
115.assumptions: Characters are UTF-16 code units. Every occurrence of a source character must map consistently, and two source characters cannot map to one target character.

example.explanation: e maps to a and g maps to d. Both occurrences of g use the same mapping, and the two source characters remain distinct.

115.baseline: Compare equality relationships for every pair of positions, costing O(n²) time.
115.approach: Maintain mappings in both directions. The forward map enforces consistency; the reverse map enforces injectivity. Together they establish a bijection between the characters actually used.
steps: Reject unequal lengths.
For each aligned pair, verify any existing forward and reverse mappings.
Store both directions if the pair is consistent.
pitfalls: A forward map alone incorrectly accepts "ab" mapping to "aa".
This models code units; Unicode code-point or grapheme-based matching needs a different iteration strategy.

116.problem: Determine whether one string can be obtained by cyclically rotating another.
116.assumptions: Lengths must match. Empty strings are rotations of each other; comparison is case-sensitive.

example.explanation: Starting at position 2 of "abcdeabcde" gives "cdeab", representing a two-place left rotation.

116.baseline: Construct and compare all n rotations, requiring O(n²) character work.
116.approach: Every rotation appears as a length-n substring of two copies of the original string. Conversely, such a substring follows the same cyclic order, so equal length plus containment is sufficient.
steps: Reject different lengths.
Concatenate the original string with itself.
Check whether the candidate occurs in that doubled string.
116.time: Conservative O(n²) worst-case substring-search bound. A KMP search over the doubled string gives O(n) worst-case time.
pitfalls: Containment without an equal-length check accepts unrelated shorter substrings.
Do not claim a guaranteed linear bound solely from calling String.contains.

117.problem: Check whether two strings contain exactly the same characters with the same multiplicities.
117.assumptions: This implementation counts Unicode code points, is case-sensitive, and does not normalize canonically equivalent Unicode forms.

example.explanation: Both strings contain three a characters and one each of n,g,r,m. Their order differs but their frequency tables agree.

117.baseline: Sort both code-point arrays and compare them in O(n log n) time.
117.approach: Increment counts for the first string and decrement them for the second. Matching multisets leave every count zero. Missing or exhausted counts can reject early.
steps: Convert each string into Unicode code points.
Reject different code-point counts.
Build the first frequency map and consume it with the second string.
117.space: O(n+m) for code-point arrays, plus O(d) counts.
pitfalls: A set loses multiplicities: "aab" and "abb" use the same set but are not anagrams.
Unicode normalization is separate from frequency equality.

118.problem: Group characters in descending order of frequency.
118.assumptions: This implementation counts Unicode code points. Ties are broken by ascending code point for deterministic output; any tie order may be accepted by a practice platform.

example.explanation: e appears twice, so both copies come first. r and t appear once; the chosen tie rule puts r before t.

118.baseline: Sort every character using its precomputed frequency as a comparator, costing O(n log n).
118.approach: Count frequencies, sort only the distinct characters, then emit each character as many times as it occurred. Sorting d distinct keys is cheaper than sorting n repeated entries when d is small.
steps: Count code-point frequencies.
Sort keys by descending count, then ascending key.
Append each key its recorded number of times.
118.time: Expected O(n+d log d), where d is the number of distinct code points.
pitfalls: Frequency sorting is different from ordinary alphabetic sorting.
A comparator that returns zero for equal frequencies is valid, but output may then depend on iteration order.

119.problem: Find the greatest number of simultaneously open parentheses in an expression.
119.assumptions: Non-parenthesis characters are ignored. This implementation rejects unbalanced parentheses.

example.explanation: Inside ((8)/4), three opening parentheses are active at once when including the outer expression parenthesis.

119.baseline: Use an explicit stack and record its maximum size, requiring O(n) space.
119.approach: For a single bracket type, only the count of unmatched opens matters. Increment on an opening bracket, decrement on a closing bracket, and retain the largest count.
steps: Start depth and maximum at zero.
Update depth on each parenthesis and detect negative depth.
After scanning, require depth zero.
pitfalls: The maximum depth is not the total number of opening parentheses.
A counter alone does not validate matching types if square or curly brackets are also included.

120.problem: Convert between canonical Roman numerals and integers.
120.assumptions: Supported values are 1 through 3999, using uppercase I,V,X,L,C,D,M and canonical subtractive pairs. Both directions are included because the sheet title requests them.

example.explanation: M contributes 1000, CM contributes 900, XC contributes 90, and IV contributes 4.

120.baseline: For decoding, separately recognize each subtractive pair; for encoding, repeatedly choose a symbol value, including those pairs.
120.approach: A Roman symbol smaller than the next symbol is subtracted; otherwise it is added. Encoding greedily uses the ordered table including 900,400,90,40,9,4. Re-encoding the decoded value verifies canonical notation.
steps: Decode with the next-symbol comparison.
Encode by repeatedly consuming the largest available table value.
For strict parsing, require the encoded result to equal the original input.
120.time: O(L) for input/output length; the canonical 1…3999 domain has bounded output length.
120.space: O(L) output; O(1) fixed lookup tables and scan state.
pitfalls: Subtract-any-smaller-symbol parsing alone accepts noncanonical forms such as IL; the round-trip check rejects them.
Zero, negative numbers, and overbar notation are outside this contract.

121.problem: Parse an initial signed decimal integer from a string, clamping overflow to the 32-bit signed range.
121.assumptions: Skip leading ordinary spaces, accept at most one optional sign, read ASCII digits until the first nondigit, and return zero when no digits are read.

example.explanation: Skip three spaces, consume the minus sign, read 4 and 2, then stop at the next space.

121.baseline: Using parseInt on the entire trimmed string rejects valid trailing text and throws rather than clamping overflow.
121.approach: Build the magnitude one digit at a time. Before multiplying by ten, compare it against (limit−digit)/10. Use magnitude limit 2147483648 for negative results because the negative int range has one extra value.
steps: Skip spaces and read a possible sign.
Accumulate consecutive digits while checking the next step for overflow.
Clamp immediately on overflow; otherwise apply the sign.
pitfalls: Check overflow before multiplication; checking an already-overflowed int is too late.
Do not resume after a nondigit: "12abc34" parses as 12.
The accepted whitespace here is a normal space, matching the usual exercise contract.

122.problem: Count contiguous ranges containing exactly k distinct values; apply the same method to substrings.
122.assumptions: The saved title says substrings, but its link is Subarrays with K Different Integers. Both wrappers are provided. Substrings are counted by position, not deduplicated by text; the string wrapper uses Unicode code points.

example.explanation: For the integer example, the valid ranges are [1,2], [1,2,1], [1,2,1,2], [2,1], [2,1,2], [1,2], and [2,3], with repeated value sequences counted at their separate positions.

122.baseline: Enumerate starts and ends while tracking distinct values, taking O(n²) time.
122.approach: Exactly k equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k−1). For an at-most window ending at right, every start from left through right is valid after shrinking, so that endpoint contributes right−left+1 ranges.
steps: Maintain frequencies inside a sliding window.
Shrink until the number of distinct keys is at most the limit.
Add the window length, then subtract the two at-most counts.
122.time: Expected O(n), since each pointer advances at most n times in each pass.
122.space: O(min(n,k+1)) window map; the string wrapper additionally allocates O(n) code points.
pitfalls: A direct exactly-k window is harder to count because many different starts can be valid.
Use long for the total, which may approach n(n+1)/2.
The title/link mismatch is retained, not silently treated as a different question.
tests: Random r=new Random(122);for(int run=0;run<100;run++){int[] a=new int[r.nextInt(12)];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)a[i]=r.nextInt(4);for(int k=1;k<=4;k++){long expected=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){Set<Integer> set=new HashSet<>();for(int j=i;j<a.length;j++){set.add(a[j]);if(set.size()==k)expected++;}}assert exactlyK(a,k)==expected;}}

123.problem: Return a longest contiguous palindromic substring without dynamic programming.
123.assumptions: Comparison is case-sensitive over UTF-16 code units. Any longest answer is acceptable; this implementation keeps the earliest found.

example.explanation: Expanding around the central a at index 1 matches b on both sides and yields "bab". The later center yields another length-three answer.

123.baseline: Enumerate all substrings and check each palindrome in O(n³) time.
123.approach: Every palindrome has either one central character or a gap between two characters. Expanding outward from all 2n−1 possible centers visits every candidate palindrome without storing a table.
steps: For each index, expand an odd center and an even center.
Use the longer expansion to compute its start and length.
Save the boundaries only when the best length improves.
123.time: O(n²) worst case, such as a string of identical characters. Manacher’s algorithm can achieve O(n), with more bookkeeping.
123.space: O(1) auxiliary state, plus O(answerLength) returned substring.
pitfalls: Checking only character centers misses even-length palindromes such as "bb".
A palindromic subsequence may skip characters; this problem requires contiguity.

124.problem: Sum the beauty of every nonempty substring, where beauty is maximum character frequency minus minimum positive character frequency.
124.assumptions: The alphabet is lowercase English letters. Characters absent from a substring are excluded from its minimum.

example.explanation: The positive-beauty substrings are "aab", "aabc", "aabcb", "abcb", and "bcb"; each has beauty one. All others contribute zero.

124.baseline: For each substring, rebuild its frequency table from scratch, taking O(n³) time.
124.approach: Fix a start index and extend the end one character at a time, updating one frequency. Scan the 26 counters to obtain the maximum and the smallest nonzero count for each extension.
steps: Start a fresh 26-counter array for each left boundary.
Increment the newly included character at each right boundary.
Add maxCount−minPositiveCount to a long total.
124.time: O(26n²), or O(n²) for the fixed alphabet.
pitfalls: Including zero-frequency letters makes almost every substring’s beauty too large.
The minimum positive frequency can change in either direction, so a simple running minimum is insufficient.

125.problem: Distinguish reversing each word’s letters from reversing the order of the words.
125.assumptions: The saved title says Reverse Every Word, but its link asks for reversed word order. Both implementations are provided. The first preserves all ordinary spaces; the second normalizes them. Text is handled as UTF-16 units.

example.output: Each word: "avaJ si nuf"; linked word-order variant: "fun is Java"
example.explanation: Reversing within intervals changes spelling while keeping positions. Reading intervals from right to left instead preserves spelling and changes their order.

125.baseline: Split into tokens and rebuild the output, but naive splitting can lose the original spacing.
125.approach: For the title’s variant, scan space-delimited intervals in a mutable character array and reverse each interval. For the linked variant, extract whole words backward and join them with single spaces.
