steps: Locate every maximal nonspace interval.
Reverse its character positions using two pointers.
Use the separate backward-word scan when solving the saved problem link.
125.space: O(n) because Java strings are immutable and a new output is produced.
pitfalls: The two interpretations produce different answers; choose the function matching the platform statement.
Reversing UTF-16 units can split surrogate pairs; use code points for full Unicode character reversal.
tests: assert reverseEachWord("Java is fun").equals("avaJ si nuf");
assert reverseWordOrder("Java is fun").equals("fun is Java");
assert reverseEachWord("  ab   cd ").equals("  ba   dc ");

126.problem: Represent a singly linked list in Java, build it from an array, and read its values from head to tail.
126.assumptions: The list ends at null and has no cycle. An empty array creates an empty list. Java uses a class for a node; there is no C++ struct or manual pointer arithmetic.

example.explanation: Each number is stored in its own Node object. The next field of 6 refers to the node holding 2, and the last next field is null.

126.baseline: An array stores values in indexed slots. A linked list stores a chain of node objects. To reach position 3, follow next from the head twice; there is no list[2] operation on this custom node chain.
126.approach:
A node needs two things: its value and a reference to the next node. head remembers the first node. tail remembers the last node while we are building the list.

Create the first node, then append each remaining value after tail and move tail forward. Keeping tail avoids walking from the head for every insertion. To read the result, use a separate current reference so head still points to the start.
steps: Create a Node class with data and next fields.
For an empty input, return null. Otherwise create the head from the first value.
Append each remaining node after tail, then move tail to the new node.
Traverse using current = current.next until current is null.
126.time: O(n) to build and O(n) to traverse.
126.space: O(n) for the new nodes. readValues also creates an O(n) result list; the traversal pointer itself uses O(1).
pitfalls: A reference names an object; assigning current = head does not copy the whole list.
Use current != null so the final node is visited. current.next != null would skip it.
Java garbage collection handles unreachable objects. Do not use C++ delete syntax.

reference.title: Singly Linked List: Structure and Basic Operations
reference.approach: Node representation and forward traversal.
reference.adaptation: The public foundation lesson gives algorithms rather than a Java tab. This Java example builds and traverses the described node chain; the node representation was also checked in the linked head-insertion lesson.

127.problem: Insert a new node before the first node of a singly linked list and return the new head.
127.assumptions: The tracker’s insertion link asks specifically for insertion at the head. The list may be empty.

example.explanation: The new node points to the old head. The rest of the chain is unchanged.

127.baseline: You could copy the values into a new structure, but head insertion needs no scan and no copying. The old head is already the attachment point.
127.approach:
Create one node and make its next field refer to the old head. Return that new node. This also handles an empty list because assigning next = null is valid.

The caller must save the returned head: head = insertHead(head, value). Changing a method’s local head variable alone does not change the caller’s variable.
steps: Allocate the new node.
Set newHead.next to the old head.
Return newHead and save it in the caller.
127.space: One new node and O(1) extra working space.
pitfalls: Link the new node to the old head before replacing your head reference.
Do not assign head.next = newHead: that inserts after the head instead of before it.

reference.title: Insert a Node at the Beginning of a Singly Linked List
reference.approach: Create a new node, link it to the old head, and return it.
reference.adaptation: The public Java node class and insertion method were checked. This version uses a static helper so the snippet can run on its own.

128.problem: Delete the supplied non-tail node from a singly linked list when you do not have the head reference.
128.assumptions: This tracker item links to LeetCode 237. The node is in the list and is not the last node. Values are unique. The task judges the resulting value sequence; it does not require that the supplied object itself becomes unreachable.

example.explanation: Copy 6 into the supplied node, then skip the following node. The supplied object remains, but the value 3 disappears.

128.baseline: If the head were available, you could find the previous node and reconnect it around the target. Here the previous node is unavailable, so that usual deletion method cannot be used.
128.approach:
The supplied node can reach the node after it. Copy that next node’s value into the supplied node, then point next to the node after the copied one. We have shortened the list by one and removed the requested value from its visible order.

This depends on there being a next node. A tail has nothing to copy, which is why the problem excludes it.
steps: Read node.next, which is guaranteed to exist.
Replace node.data with that next node’s data.
Set node.next to node.next.next.
pitfalls: This differs from deleting a value when the head is available. Check which inputs the problem gives you.
The physical object removed from the chain is the following node. Object identity matters in applications that keep other references.
The method cannot delete the tail under this contract.

129.problem: Count how many nodes are in a singly linked list.
129.assumptions: The list is finite and ends at null. An empty list has length 0.

example.explanation: Visit the nodes holding 4, 1 and 8. The null after 8 is not a node.

129.baseline: A recursive solution can count 1 plus the length of the rest of the list. That uses one call per node and can overflow the Java call stack on long input.
129.approach: Keep a counter and walk through the chain. Each time current refers to a node, add one and move to current.next. When current becomes null, every node has been counted once. The values themselves do not matter.
steps: Set count = 0 and current = head.
While current is not null, increment count and advance current.
Return count.
pitfalls: Use current != null, not current.next != null; the latter misses the last node and fails on an empty list.
A cycle never reaches null. Cycle detection is a separate question.
tests: Node a=new Node(4);a.next=new Node(1);a.next.next=new Node(8);assert length(a)==3;assert a.data==4;
Node head=null;for(int i=0;i<100000;i++){Node x=new Node(i);x.next=head;head=x;}assert length(head)==100000;

reference.title: Find the length of the Linked List
reference.approach: Count nodes using the forward traversal described in the singly linked-list foundation lesson.
reference.adaptation: The public problem and its empty-list constraint were checked. No public Java editorial was used; this is an original iterative implementation.

130.problem: Return true if a linked list contains the requested key, otherwise return false.
130.assumptions: The list ends at null. Values do not need to be sorted. This implementation also returns false for an empty list.

example.explanation: The first value is 5, so continue. The second value is 2, so stop and return true.

130.baseline: Copying the values into an array would still require visiting the nodes first. For a single search, compare values during that visit instead.
130.approach:
Start at the head and compare each node’s data with the key. A match answers the question immediately. If you reach null without a match, there are no nodes left to check.

Do not use binary search on this chain. Reaching a middle node already takes a walk, and the input is not promised to be sorted.
steps: Start current at head.
Return true as soon as current.data equals key.
Otherwise advance to next; return false when the chain ends.
130.time: O(n) in the worst case; O(1) for a match at the head.
pitfalls: Compare the stored integer, not the Node object itself, with the key.
Missing values require checking the whole list.
tests: Node a=new Node(5);a.next=new Node(2);a.next.next=new Node(7);assert contains(a,2);assert contains(a,5);assert contains(a,7);assert !contains(a,9);

reference.title: Search in Linked List
reference.approach: Visit nodes in order and stop when the key matches.
reference.adaptation: The public problem requires a boolean result. This Java follows the foundation lesson’s traversal; no public Java editorial was used.

131.problem: Represent a doubly linked list in Java and build it from an array.
131.assumptions: Every node has data, prev and next. The head’s prev and the tail’s next are null. Empty input returns null.

example.explanation: From 8, next reaches 2 and prev reaches 3. Each connection works in both directions.

131.baseline: A singly linked list has only next links. Adding prev uses one more reference per node and lets us move backwards without searching from the head.
131.approach:
Create the first node and remember it as both head and tail. For every remaining value, create a new node. Connect tail.next to it and its prev back to tail, then move tail to the new node.

Both assignments matter. A list can look correct when walking forward but still be broken when walking backward if one prev link is missing.
steps: Create a node class with data, prev and next.
Build the first node, or return null for an empty array.
For each new node, connect the old tail and new node in both directions.
Return head; it remains the first node throughout the build.
131.space: O(n) for the resulting nodes and O(1) working space.
pitfalls: For adjacent nodes a and b, a.next == b should agree with b.prev == a.
A Java Node reference is not an integer memory address.
Do not confuse null at an endpoint with a node whose value is zero.
tests: assert fromArray(new int[]{})==null;Node a=fromArray(new int[]{4});assert a.prev==null&&a.next==null;

int[] values=new int[100];for(int i=0;i<100;i++)values[i]=i;Node head=fromArray(values),tail=head;for(int i=0;i<100;i++){assert tail.data==i;if(i<99){assert tail.next.prev==tail;tail=tail.next;}}for(int i=99;i>=0;i--){assert tail.data==i;tail=tail.prev;}assert tail==null;

reference.title: Doubly Linked List: Structure and Basic Operations
reference.approach: Build a doubly linked list by connecting each new node in both directions.
reference.adaptation: The public foundation lesson gives steps rather than Java code. This standalone Java implements those steps.

132.problem: Insert a new node before the head of a doubly linked list and return the new head.
132.assumptions: The tracker’s generic DLL insertion title links to insertion before the head. The existing list has consistent prev and next links. Empty input is also supported.

example.explanation: The new 2 points forward to 6, and 6 points backward to 2. The new head’s prev stays null.

132.baseline: No traversal is needed: the head reference already tells us where the new node belongs.
132.approach: This is singly linked head insertion plus one backward link. Create the node, point its next at the old head, and, when the old head exists, point its prev back at the new node. Return the new node. The old values and links after the head stay in the same order.
steps: Create the new node with prev initially null.
Set its next to the current head.
If the old head exists, set oldHead.prev to the new node.
Return the new node.
132.space: One new node and O(1) extra working space.
pitfalls: Forgetting oldHead.prev breaks backward traversal.
Save the returned head in the caller.
Check head != null before writing head.prev.
tests: Node head=null;for(int i=0;i<100;i++)head=insertBeforeHead(head,i);Node p=head;for(int i=99;i>=0;i--){assert p.data==i;if(p.next!=null)assert p.next.prev==p;p=p.next;}assert p==null;

reference.title: Doubly Linked List: Structure and Basic Operations
reference.approach: Insert before the head by updating both forward and backward links.
reference.adaptation: The foundation steps and the tracker-linked insert-before-head problem were checked. The foundation page has no Java tab; this is an original implementation of its steps.

133.problem: Remove the first node of a doubly linked list and return the new head.
133.assumptions: The tracker’s DLL deletion link asks for head deletion. The existing links are consistent. Empty input returns null.

example.explanation: Move head from 2 to 5, then clear 5.prev because 5 is now the first node.

133.baseline: The node to remove is already known, so there is no need to search. Rebuilding the list would add work without helping.
133.approach:
Save the next node as the new head. If it exists, set its prev to null. Disconnect the old head’s next and return the new head. Removing the only node returns null.

Java does not need a delete statement. Once an object is unreachable, it is eligible for garbage collection. Clearing a link updates the list structure; it does not force memory to be freed immediately.
steps: Return null immediately if head is null.
Save head.next as newHead.
Clear newHead.prev if newHead exists, and detach the old head.
Return newHead.
pitfalls: The new head must have prev == null.
After deleting a single-node list, newHead is null, so do not dereference it.

reference.title: Doubly Linked List: Structure and Basic Operations
reference.approach: Delete the head and clear the new head’s backward link.
reference.adaptation: The public foundation steps and the tracker-linked delete-head problem were checked. This Java implements those steps using garbage collection instead of manual deletion.

134.problem: Reverse a doubly linked list by changing its links and return the new head.
134.assumptions: The list ends at null, has no cycle, and its next/prev links agree. Empty input returns null. Node values are preserved.

example.explanation: The old tail becomes the new head. Every next arrow and prev arrow trades direction.

134.baseline: You could store node references in an array and reconnect them in reverse order, using O(n) extra space. Swapping the two references inside each node needs only a few temporary variables.
134.approach:
At each node, save its original next reference. Then swap next and prev. After the swap, moving through next would send us backwards, so continue using the original next that we saved.

Keep newHead pointing to the most recently processed node. The final processed node was the old tail, so it is the correct new head. Its new prev is null, just as the old tail’s next was null.
steps: Set current to head and newHead to null.
Save originalNext before changing any link.
Swap current.next and current.prev, then remember current as newHead.
Move to originalNext. Return newHead when current becomes null.
134.space: O(1); the existing nodes are reused.
pitfalls: Changing only next leaves the backward chain wrong.
Continue through the saved original next, not the swapped next.
Reversing values alone does not reverse node order. This solution preserves each node’s data.
tests: Node a=new Node(4),b=new Node(7),c=new Node(2);a.next=b;b.prev=a;b.next=c;c.prev=b;Node head=reverseDLL(a);assert head==c&&c.prev==null&&c.next==b&&b.prev==c&&b.next==a&&a.prev==b&&a.next==null;assert a.data==4&&b.data==7&&c.data==2;

for(int n=1;n<=100;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0){nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];nodes[i].prev=nodes[i-1];}}Node head=reverseDLL(nodes[0]),p=head;for(int i=n-1;i>=0;i--){assert p==nodes[i];assert p.prev==(i==n-1?null:nodes[i+1]);p=p.next;}assert p==null;assert reverseDLL(head)==nodes[0];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)assert nodes[i].next==(i+1==n?null:nodes[i+1]);}

reference.title: Reverse a Doubly Linked List
reference.approach: Reverse the existing nodes in place by exchanging their prev and next links.
reference.adaptation: The public problem was checked. It does not expose a Java editorial in the sheet; this is an original, tested pointer-swap implementation.

135.problem: Return the middle node of a linked list. For an even-length list, return the second of the two middle nodes.
135.assumptions: The list is finite and has no cycle. The tracker links to LeetCode 876, which returns a node reference. This implementation also returns null for an empty list.

example.explanation: There are four nodes. The two middle nodes hold 4 and 6; the required second middle is 6.

135.baseline: Count n nodes in one pass, then move n / 2 steps from the head. That reaches the required node in a second pass.
135.approach:
Let slow move one node per turn and fast move two. After two turns, slow has moved two places while fast has moved four. When fast runs out of list, slow has covered half of it.

Starting both references at head and allowing fast to become null makes the even-length case return the second middle. We return slow itself, so the caller can still access the nodes after it.
steps: Set slow and fast to head.
While fast and fast.next both exist, advance slow once and fast twice.
Return slow.
pitfalls: Check fast != null before reading fast.next. Java && stops at the first false condition.
Returning slow.data answers a different return contract. The tracker’s linked problem needs slow.
tests: Node a=new Node(2),b=new Node(4),d=new Node(6),e=new Node(8);a.next=b;b.next=d;d.next=e;assert middle(a)==d;assert middleByCounting(a)==d;
assert middle(null)==null;assert middleByCounting(null)==null;Node a=new Node(9);assert middle(a)==a;

for(int n=1;n<=101;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(7);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}assert middle(nodes[0])==nodes[n/2];assert middleByCounting(nodes[0])==nodes[n/2];}

reference.title: Find Middle of Linked List
reference.approach: Count and walk, then use slow/fast pointers to reach the second middle.
reference.adaptation: Both Java variants were checked. The article returns data; the tracker-linked problem returns a node, so both methods here return Node. The article’s C++-style if (!head) in Java is replaced with a valid null-safe implementation.

135.baselineTime: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; two passes.

136.problem: Reverse a singly linked list by changing next links, then return its new head.
136.assumptions: The list has no cycle. Empty input returns null. The final solution reuses the same node objects and keeps their data unchanged.

example.explanation: The original node holding 1 becomes the head. The original 3 becomes the tail and points to null.

136.baseline: Striver first shows a stack of values: save every value, then pop them back into the existing nodes. This reverses the value sequence but leaves node order unchanged. It uses O(n) extra space.
136.approach:
Keep prev at the front of the part already reversed and current at the next node to process. Before changing current.next, save it as next. Otherwise we would lose the rest of the original chain.

Point current.next back to prev, then move prev to current and current to the saved next. Each turn transfers one node from the remaining chain to the front of the reversed chain. When no nodes remain, prev is the new head.
steps: Start prev at null and current at head.
Save next = current.next.
Point current.next to prev, then advance prev and current.
Return prev after current becomes null.
pitfalls: Save the original next before overwriting the link.
The first processed node must point to null; that is why prev starts at null.
Stack-based value rewriting does not preserve the data attached to each object. Use link reversal when node identity matters.
tests: Node a=new Node(3),b=new Node(7),d=new Node(1);a.next=b;b.next=d;Node h=reverse(a);assert h==d&&d.next==b&&b.next==a&&a.next==null;assert a.data==3&&b.data==7&&d.data==1;

for(int n=1;n<=100;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}Node p=reverse(nodes[0]);for(int i=n-1;i>=0;i--){assert p==nodes[i]&&p.data==i;p=p.next;}assert p==null;}
Node a=new Node(3),b=new Node(7),d=new Node(1);a.next=b;b.next=d;assert reverseValues(a)==a;assert a.data==1&&b.data==7&&d.data==3&&a.next==b&&b.next==d;

137.problem: Reverse a singly linked list using recursion and return its new head.
137.assumptions: This is the tracker’s separate recursive version of list reversal. The list is finite and has no cycle. Use the iterative version for very long lists to avoid Java stack overflow.

example.explanation: First reverse 8 → 5 into 5 → 8. Then connect 8 back to 2 and clear 2.next.

137.baseline: The previous question reverses links in a loop using O(1) extra space. Here the call stack remembers the unfinished nodes instead.
137.approach:
Ask the recursive call to reverse everything after head. When it returns, the old second node is the tail of that reversed part. Its next should now point back to head. Then clear head.next, because head becomes the new tail.

The new head comes from the recursive call and stays the same while the calls return. Empty and single-node lists are already reversed, so they stop the recursion.
steps: Return head when it is null or its next is null.
Save newHead = reverseRecursive(head.next).
Set head.next.next = head, then head.next = null.
Return newHead.
pitfalls: Clearing head.next is essential. Without it, the last two nodes point at each other and create a cycle.
Return newHead, not head, while unwinding.
The source’s current public article shows iterative Java and mentions recursion only in its follow-up; this saved lesson supplies the recursive variant required by the tracker.
tests: Node a=new Node(2),b=new Node(8),d=new Node(5);a.next=b;b.next=d;Node h=reverseRecursive(a);assert h==d&&d.next==b&&b.next==a&&a.next==null;

for(int n=1;n<=200;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}Node p=reverseRecursive(nodes[0]);for(int i=n-1;i>=0;i--){assert p==nodes[i]&&p.data==i;p=p.next;}assert p==null;}

138.problem: Return whether following next links eventually revisits the same node.
138.assumptions: The list may be empty or contain a cycle. Compare Node references, not their integer data. Do not change any next link.

example.explanation: The walk repeats 7 → 2 → 9 forever. Repeated values alone would not prove a cycle; the same node must be revisited.

138.baseline: Keep a set of visited Node references. Finding a reference already in the set proves that the walk has returned to an earlier node. Reaching null proves there is no cycle.
138.approach:
Move slow one node per turn and fast two. If there is no cycle, fast reaches the end. If there is a cycle, both pointers eventually enter it. Inside the loop, fast gains one position on slow each turn, so it must catch slow within one lap.

Compare them after moving. They start together at head, which by itself says nothing about whether a cycle exists.
steps: Start slow and fast at head.
While fast and fast.next exist, move slow once and fast twice.
Return true if the references meet after a move.
Return false when fast reaches the end.
138.time: O(n), where n is the number of reachable distinct nodes.
pitfalls: Check equality after the first move, not before it.
A single node can have a cycle when its next points to itself.
Storing or comparing only data falsely detects cycles when separate nodes have equal values.
tests: Node a=new Node(4),b=new Node(7),d=new Node(2),e=new Node(9);a.next=b;b.next=d;d.next=e;e.next=b;assert hasCycle(a)&&hasCycleWithSet(a);assert e.next==b;

for(int n=1;n<=50;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(5);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}assert !hasCycle(nodes[0])&&!hasCycleWithSet(nodes[0]);for(int entry=0;entry<n;entry++){nodes[n-1].next=nodes[entry];assert hasCycle(nodes[0])&&hasCycleWithSet(nodes[0]);for(int i=0;i<n-1;i++)assert nodes[i].next==nodes[i+1];assert nodes[n-1].next==nodes[entry];}}

139.problem: Return the node where a linked-list cycle begins, or null if there is no cycle.
139.assumptions: The list may be empty or contain a cycle. Compare Node references, not their integer data. Do not change any next link.

example.explanation: The first traversal enters the repeating part at 7. The answer is that node reference, not a new node with the same data.

139.baseline: Walk with a set of visited references. The first repeated reference is the cycle entry. This uses O(n) extra space.
139.approach:
First use slow and fast to find a meeting inside the cycle. Then reset slow to head and leave fast at the meeting point. Move both one step per turn. Their next meeting is the cycle entry.

Why does resetting work? Let a be the distance before the cycle, b the distance from the entry to the first meeting, and L the loop length. When they meet, fast has travelled twice as far as slow. Its extra distance is a whole number of laps, so a + b is a multiple of L. Starting at that meeting, another a steps therefore lands at the entry. The pointer from head also needs exactly a steps.
steps: Find a slow/fast meeting, returning null if fast reaches the end.
Reset slow to head; keep fast at the meeting.
Move both one step until their references agree.
Return that shared reference without changing the list.
pitfalls: The first meeting may be anywhere in the cycle. Do not return it immediately.
After the reset, both pointers move one step; fast no longer moves two.
A cycle that begins at head may need zero moves in the second phase.
tests: for(int n=1;n<=50;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(5);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}assert cycleStart(nodes[0])==null&&cycleStartWithSet(nodes[0])==null;for(int entry=0;entry<n;entry++){nodes[n-1].next=nodes[entry];assert cycleStart(nodes[0])==nodes[entry];assert cycleStartWithSet(nodes[0])==nodes[entry];assert nodes[n-1].next==nodes[entry];}}

140.problem: Count the distinct nodes inside a linked-list cycle. Return 0 if there is no cycle.
140.assumptions: The list may be empty or contain a cycle. Compare Node references, not their integer data. Do not change any next link.

example.explanation: Only 7, 2 and 9 belong to the loop. The node holding 4 is before the loop and is not counted.

140.baseline: Save visited references until one repeats. Starting at that repeated node, walk one full lap and count its nodes. The set needs O(n) space.
140.approach:
Use slow and fast to find any meeting inside the loop. Keep that meeting reference fixed and walk another pointer from its next node until it returns to the meeting. Start the count at 1 because the meeting node itself already counts.

There is no need to find the entry first. A complete lap contains the same number of nodes regardless of where in the loop you start.
steps: Run slow/fast cycle detection. Return 0 if fast reaches the end.
At a meeting, set length = 1 and current = meeting.next.
Advance current and count until current is the meeting node again.
Return the count.
pitfalls: Do not include the nodes before the loop.
Count the meeting node once, not zero times or twice.
Only call countLap after confirming its argument lies inside a cycle.
tests: for(int n=1;n<=50;n++){Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(5);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}assert cycleLength(nodes[0])==0&&cycleLengthWithSet(nodes[0])==0;for(int entry=0;entry<n;entry++){nodes[n-1].next=nodes[entry];assert cycleLength(nodes[0])==n-entry;assert cycleLengthWithSet(nodes[0])==n-entry;assert nodes[n-1].next==nodes[entry];}}

141.problem: Check whether the linked-list values read the same forwards and backwards.
141.assumptions: The list is finite and has no cycle. An empty or single-node list is a palindrome. Restore all original links before returning, even when there is a mismatch.

example.explanation: Compare the outer 3s and then the 8s. The middle 5 needs no partner.

141.baseline: Push all values onto a stack, then walk from head again while popping. The stack gives values in reverse order, so any mismatch returns false.
141.approach:
Find the end of the first half using slow and fast pointers. Reverse the part after slow. Now the end of the list can be read in forward steps, alongside the beginning.

Compare one node from each side until the reversed half ends. For odd length, the unpaired middle stays in the first half and is not compared. Remember the result, reverse the second half back, and reconnect it. A check should not leave the caller’s list cut or reversed.
steps: Find the first-half endpoint with slow/fast pointers.
Reverse slow.next and keep its returned head.
Compare from head and from the reversed half, stopping on a mismatch.
Restore slow.next by reversing that half again, then return the comparison result.
pitfalls: The first-half endpoint loop differs from the second-middle loop: it checks fast.next and fast.next.next.
Restore before returning false too.
Compare data values for a palindrome; compare references for cycle detection.
tests: int[] values={3,8,5,8,3};Node[] nodes=new Node[5];for(int i=0;i<5;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}assert isPalindrome(nodes[0])&&palindromeWithStack(nodes[0]);for(int i=0;i<5;i++)assert nodes[i].next==(i==4?null:nodes[i+1]);

Random r=new Random(141);for(int run=0;run<400;run++){int n=1+r.nextInt(30);Node[] nodes=new Node[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){nodes[i]=new Node(r.nextInt(5));if(i>0)nodes[i-1].next=nodes[i];}if(run%2==0)for(int i=0;i<n/2;i++)nodes[n-1-i].data=nodes[i].data;boolean expected=palindromeWithStack(nodes[0]);int[] data=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)data[i]=nodes[i].data;assert isPalindrome(nodes[0])==expected;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){assert nodes[i].next==(i+1==n?null:nodes[i+1]);assert nodes[i].data==data[i];}}

reference.approach: Stack comparison, then reverse, compare and restore the second half.
reference.adaptation: Both Java approaches were checked. The source declares data but compares val in its optimal snippet; this version consistently uses data. Restoration runs through one shared exit path.

142.problem: Group nodes at odd positions first, then nodes at even positions, keeping order within each group.
142.assumptions: The tracker links to LeetCode 328: positions start at 1. The current Striver article instead groups even VALUES before odd values. These are different tasks. oddEvenPositions solves the tracker; evenValuesFirst below solves the article variant.

example.explanation: Positions 1, 3 and 5 hold 4, 3 and 1. The article’s value-based rule would instead give 4 → 8 → 6 → 3 → 1.

142.baseline: For the position-based task, collect references at odd positions and then even positions in an array, then reconnect them. That uses O(n) space. The linked article’s array baseline groups values, so it solves the other variant.
142.approach:
For the tracker, keep odd at the last odd-position node and even at the last even-position node. Save the first even node before changing links. Skip over the opposite group each time: connect odd to even.next, then connect even to the next even-position node. Finally attach the even chain after the odd chain.

For the article’s different rule, inspect data % 2 instead. Build an even-value chain and an odd-value chain, detach each node before appending it, and join even before odd. Both methods preserve each group’s original order and reuse the nodes.
steps: For the tracker, set odd = head, even = head.next, and save evenHead.
While another odd-position node exists, extend the odd chain and then the even chain.
Join odd.next to evenHead.
Use the separately labelled evenValuesFirst method only when grouping depends on values.
pitfalls: Odd/even position is not odd/even data. Use an example where they differ.
Save evenHead before moving even.
A leftover old next link can create a cycle when building separate chains; detach nodes before appending.
tests: int[] values={4,8,3,6,1};Node[] a=new Node[5];for(int i=0;i<5;i++){a[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=oddEvenPositions(a[0]);for(int i:new int[]{0,2,4,1,3}){assert p==a[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;

int[] values={4,8,3,6,1};Node[] a=new Node[5];for(int i=0;i<5;i++){a[i]=new Node(values[i]);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=evenValuesFirst(a[0]);for(int i:new int[]{0,1,3,2,4}){assert p==a[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;

143.problem: Remove the nth node counted from the end of a linked list and return its updated head.
143.assumptions: The list is finite. n = 1 means the last node. Valid input has 1 ≤ n ≤ length; this implementation rejects invalid n without changing the chain.

example.explanation: Counting from the end gives 8 first and 2 second. Remove the node holding 2.

143.baseline: Count the length, then start from a dummy node and walk length − n steps. That leaves you immediately before the node to remove.
143.approach:
Put a dummy node before head. Start fast and slow at the dummy, then move fast n steps. Keep that gap as both move forward. When fast reaches the last node, slow is immediately before the target. Bypass slow.next.

The dummy also handles removing the head: slow can stay on the dummy, and changing dummy.next gives the new head. The dummy is not part of the returned list.
steps: Create a dummy whose next is head.
Advance fast n times, rejecting n if it runs past the list.
Move fast and slow together until fast.next is null.
Skip slow.next and return dummy.next.
143.time: O(n), where n here means the list length.
pitfalls: The gap and stopping condition belong together: with both starting at dummy and a gap of n, stop when fast.next is null.
Save the returned head because the first node may be removed.
tests: Node a=new Node(3),b=new Node(7),d=new Node(2),e=new Node(8);a.next=b;b.next=d;d.next=e;assert removeNth(a,2)==a&&b.next==e;

for(int size=1;size<=35;size++)for(int n=1;n<=size;n++)for(int method=0;method<2;method++){Node[] a=new Node[size];for(int i=0;i<size;i++){a[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=method==0?removeNth(a[0],n):removeNthByCounting(a[0],n);for(int i=0;i<size;i++)if(i!=size-n){assert p==a[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;}

144.problem: Delete the middle node of a linked list. For even length, delete the second middle.
144.assumptions: The middle has zero-based index length / 2. A single-node list becomes empty. Empty input also returns null.

example.explanation: The four-node list has middle index 2, so the node holding 8 is removed.

144.baseline: Count the nodes, calculate length / 2, and walk to the node before that index. Reconnect it around the middle.
144.approach:
Use slow and fast as in the middle-node question, but remember previous as well. Before moving slow, save its old position in previous. When fast finishes, slow is the middle and previous is the node that must skip it.

Handle zero or one node first. Then previous is guaranteed to exist when deletion happens, because a list of at least two nodes advances slow at least once.
steps: Return null for an empty or single-node list.
Start slow and fast at head, with previous = null.
Before each slow step, set previous = slow; move slow once and fast twice.
Set previous.next = slow.next and return head.
pitfalls: The even-length convention is the second middle, not the first.
Save previous before moving slow.
The single-node case has no previous node and needs its early return.
tests: Node a=new Node(5),b=new Node(2),d=new Node(8),e=new Node(4);a.next=b;b.next=d;d.next=e;assert deleteMiddle(a)==a&&b.next==e;

for(int size=1;size<=100;size++)for(int method=0;method<2;method++){Node[] a=new Node[size];for(int i=0;i<size;i++){a[i]=new Node(i);if(i>0)a[i-1].next=a[i];}Node p=method==0?deleteMiddle(a[0]):deleteMiddleByCounting(a[0]);for(int i=0;i<size;i++)if(i!=size/2){assert p==a[i];p=p.next;}assert p==null;}

reference.approach: Count to locate the predecessor, then track it during a slow/fast traversal.
